Use when founders struggle with motivation beyond profit, when leadership feels like burden rather than calling, when building a culture of accountability and mutual obligation, when navigating tensions between personal ambition and collective responsibility, or when aligning team purpose with organisational mission.

commands.name: foreman:stoic-emotional-mastery
commands.description: (foreman) Applies the Stoic approach to emotions -- not suppression but reframing -- to entrepreneurial leadership. Covers the distinction between first impressions and considered judgments, Seneca's anger management method, the practice of responding rather than reacting, and the Stoic treatment of fear, desire, pleasure, and grief. Use when anger is clouding judgment, fear is driving decisions, desire is distorting priorities, struggling to separate emotional reactions from rational assessment, or seeking a philosophical alternative to conventional emotional intelligence models.

commands.name: foreman:stoic-fortitude-and-resilience
commands.description: (foreman) Provides the philosophical foundations of inner strength, endurance, and anti-fragility drawn from Stoic thought, teaching entrepreneurs why hardship strengthens character, how to prepare mentally for adversity through voluntary discomfort, and why patience and perseverance outperform luck as long-term competitive assets. Use when facing sustained business adversity, preparing mentally for a high-stakes launch or fundraise, building psychological toughness before a difficult transition, questioning whether a setback signals failure or formation, or seeking the philosophical basis for resilience practices covered in leader-resilience-and-wellbeing.

commands.name: foreman:stoic-mortality-and-perspective
commands.description: (foreman) Applies the Stoic practice of memento mori -- meditation on mortality -- as a tool for entrepreneurial clarity, urgency, and perspective. Teaches how the awareness of death sharpens focus, eliminates trivial distractions, accelerates decision-making, informs legacy thinking, and provides the 'view from above' that rescales problems to their actual size. Use when an entrepreneur is paralysed by indecision, when petty concerns are consuming disproportionate energy, when time management lacks urgency, when succession or legacy questions arise, when perspective has been lost to operational detail, or when the founder needs the ultimate clarifying question: what would matter if this were the last year?

commands.name: foreman:stoic-pragmatism
commands.description: (foreman) Distills the Stoic insistence on philosophy as action rather than theory, covering simplicity, efficiency, realism, the primacy of practice over abstraction, and the elimination of unnecessary complexity. Use when founders are overthinking strategy at the expense of execution, when organisations are drowning in process without progress, when the gap between stated philosophy and daily behaviour needs closing, or when a team needs to cut through complexity and focus on what actually works.

commands.name: foreman:stoic-problem-solving
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches Marcus Aurelius's central method for converting obstacles into advantages, covering the reverse clause, creative reframing, persistence under adversity, and the discipline of focused action. Use when a startup faces setbacks that feel terminal, when market conditions shift against you, when key plans fail and alternatives seem absent, or when the team needs a framework for resilience and resourcefulness under pressure.

commands.name: foreman:stoic-right-action
commands.description: (foreman) Applies Stoic ethics of right action to entrepreneurial decision-making, covering the four cardinal virtues (courage, justice, temperance, wisdom), ethical leadership under pressure, and the discipline of choosing the harder right over the easier wrong. Use when facing ethical dilemmas in business, building a values-driven culture, making decisions with imperfect information, navigating conflicts between profit and principle, or establishing personal and organizational codes of conduct.

commands.name: foreman:stoic-self-awareness
commands.description: (foreman) Applies Stoic practices of self-examination to entrepreneurial leadership, drawing on Seneca's evening review, Epictetus's teaching on honest self-assessment, and Marcus Aurelius's private journaling discipline. Covers blind spots, the gap between self-image and reality, integration of character, and continuous philosophical self-scrutiny. Use when suspecting blind spots in leadership, receiving feedback that contradicts self-image, seeking a structured introspection practice, struggling with integrity under pressure, or building habits of ongoing self-examination.

commands.name: foreman:stoic-unbiased-thought
commands.description: (foreman) Applies the Stoic discipline of objective perception to entrepreneurial thinking, drawing on Marcus Aurelius's practice of describing things in their simplest terms, the 'view from above' technique, and the Stoic method of stripping value judgments from events. Covers cognitive distortions through a Stoic lens, the difference between observation and interpretation, and the practice of seeing things as they are. Use when distorted thinking is driving poor decisions, when hype or panic is clouding judgment, when strong opinions need stress-testing, or when seeking objectivity amid emotionally charged situations.

commands.name: foreman:stoic-virtue-and-kindness
commands.description: (foreman) Presents the Stoic argument that character is the ultimate competitive advantage and that virtue -- encompassing honesty, kindness, justice, and moral courage -- is not a means to success but constitutes success itself. Use when an entrepreneur faces ethical dilemmas, when competitive pressure tempts shortcuts, when building company culture around values rather than metrics, when kindness is dismissed as weakness in a high-stakes environment, or when seeking philosophical grounding for why doing right and doing well are the same endeavour.

commands.name: foreman:story-beginnings-and-endings
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches the opposite-of-the-end rule for finding a story's beginning, the discipline of starting as close to the end as possible, the use of forward movement in opening lines, and the art of frayed endings that resonate without neatly resolving. Use when a pitch or talk starts in the wrong place, when an audience loses interest in the first thirty seconds, when a story's conclusion feels forced or anticlimactic, or when refining any narrative for maximum structural impact.

commands.name: foreman:story-performance-and-delivery
commands.description: (foreman) Covers the practical mechanics of performing a story: present tense as default, tense shifting, the two strategies for telling success stories without sounding like a braggart, scene-based memorisation, eye contact, microphone technique, emotional control, word selection, and adapting delivery across contexts from stages to boardrooms. Use when preparing to deliver a story live, when rehearsing a pitch or keynote, or when a narrative reads well on paper but falls flat in the room.

commands.name: foreman:story-structure-and-arc
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches the five-second moment principle, the relationship between surface spectacle and underlying transformation, and the But and Therefore technique for creating narrative momentum. Use when a pitch or presentation feels flat despite containing good material, when a founder's narrative lacks forward movement, when replacing chronological recounting with cause-and-effect storytelling, or when diagnosing why an audience disengages midway through a talk.

commands.name: foreman:storytelling-for-leaders
commands.description: (foreman) Equips leaders with practical storytelling techniques for driving organisational change, building empathy, simplifying complexity, and creating shared narratives. Use when launching a transformation initiative, when data alone fails to persuade, when teams need emotional alignment around a vision, or when a leader's communication is technically sound but fails to move people.

commands.name: foreman:storytelling-truth-and-vividness
commands.description: (foreman) Provides an ethical framework for nonfiction storytelling (the Five Permissible Lies) and techniques for creating vivid mental imagery (Cinema of the Mind). Applies when a founder is crafting a company origin story, preparing a keynote, refining a customer case study, or deciding how much to compress or omit from a real narrative. Use when the question is not what to say but how truthfully and vividly to say it.

commands.name: foreman:strategic-questioning
commands.description: (foreman) Transforms leaders from directive communicators into strategic questioners who use inquiry to inspire thinking, surface hidden problems, build ownership, and drive better decisions. Covers five essential leadership questions, the art of context-rich inquiry, question-driven meeting design, and techniques for using questions to lead without dictating. Use when meetings produce compliance instead of commitment, when teams wait for answers instead of generating them, when a leader talks more than they listen, when preparing for difficult or ambiguous decisions, or when building a culture of curiosity.

commands.name: foreman:strategic-thinking-and-alignment
commands.description: (foreman) Develops the daily habits and communication practices that separate strategic leaders from operational ones. Covers carving out time for strategic thinking, communicating strategic changes effectively, building organisational alignment, challenging the status quo, and fostering competitive innovation without duplicating formal strategy frameworks. Use when feeling trapped in operational detail, struggling to communicate a strategic shift, discovering that teams are pursuing divergent goals, preparing for strategy offsites, or sensing that the organisation is coasting on inertia.

commands.name: foreman:swot-pest-analysis
commands.description: (foreman) Conducts integrated SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) and PEST (Political, Economic, Social, Technological) strategic analysis. Generates actionable strategies through the TOWS matrix by crossing internal capabilities with external forces. Use when evaluating market entry, preparing board strategy sessions, assessing competitive positioning, scanning the macro environment for regulatory or economic shifts, or generating evidence-backed strategic options.

commands.name: foreman:systems-thinking
commands.description: (foreman) Analyzes complex business problems through systems thinking by mapping causal loops, identifying reinforcing and balancing feedback dynamics, and diagnosing system archetypes like Fixes That Fail, Shifting the Burden, and Limits to Growth. Use when quick fixes keep backfiring, growth plateaus unexpectedly, departments optimize locally at the expense of the whole, or interventions produce unintended consequences across the organization.

commands.name: foreman:teaching-and-leading
commands.description: (foreman) Guides founders in leading through modelling behaviour, coaching (not managing), leveraging mirror neurons for mood contagion, distributing leadership titles generously, and using gratitude as a pre-meeting performance enhancer. Covers showing rather than telling, strengths-based leadership, the coach-and-student mindset, external accountability systems, vision-people-resources leadership triad, delivering bad news transparently, energy-state management, and making everyone a leader. Use when onboarding a first direct report, preparing to deliver difficult news to a team, noticing declining team morale, struggling with micromanagement tendencies, or building a leadership culture in an early-stage company.

commands.name: foreman:team-culture-and-dynamics
commands.description: (foreman) Provides daily practices for reading team energy, shaping culture deliberately, writing unwritten rules, diagnosing accountability gaps, balancing personality types, and building high-performing teams through social connection. Use when a team feels stuck or stale, when collaboration derails despite good intentions, when unwritten norms produce confusion, when new hires struggle to decode the culture, or when a leader suspects the team's vibe is off but cannot articulate why.

commands.name: foreman:thinking-fast-and-slow
commands.description: (foreman) Audits business decisions for cognitive biases using Kahneman's dual-process theory of System 1 (fast, intuitive) and System 2 (slow, analytical) thinking. Covers overconfidence, anchoring, loss aversion, planning fallacy, and availability heuristic. Use when conducting pre-mortems on major initiatives, debiasing fundraising projections, applying reference-class forecasting, sorting decisions by required processing mode, or building structured decision protocols.

commands.name: foreman:thomas-kilmann-conflict
commands.description: (foreman) Diagnoses and resolves conflicts using the Thomas-Kilmann five-mode framework: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, and accommodating, mapped across assertiveness and cooperativeness dimensions. Use when navigating co-founder disagreements, mediating cross-functional team friction, choosing the right conflict mode for high-stakes decisions, expanding personal conflict style range, or designing conflict resolution processes for the organization.

commands.name: foreman:tipping-point
commands.description: (foreman) Analyzes viral growth potential using Gladwell's Tipping Point framework through three rules: the Law of the Few (Connectors, Mavens, Salespeople), the Stickiness Factor, and the Power of Context. Use when product growth is stubbornly linear despite high satisfaction, designing launch strategies for organic adoption, engineering shareable product moments, identifying key influencers in a target market, or diagnosing why a superior product fails to spread.

commands.name: foreman:tone-and-engagement
commands.description: (foreman) Diagnoses and corrects the tonal failures that cause business writing to anaesthetise readers rather than persuade them. Addresses passive voice, nominalizations, hyperformality, sarcasm, and the specific calibration of tone to audience and relationship. Use when drafting client communications, revising documents that feel lifeless or overly formal, preparing sensitive messages that require tonal precision, or building writing standards for a team.

commands.name: foreman:tough-decision-situations
commands.description: (foreman) Addresses the four hardest decision scenarios founders face: teams that cannot reach consensus, choices where every option is bad, decisions that have already gone wrong, and calls that must be made under severe time pressure. Provides structured techniques for each scenario including disagree-and-commit protocols, least-worst analysis, early admission and course-correction frameworks, and recognition-primed decision heuristics. Use when the team is deadlocked and unable to converge, when all available options carry significant downside, when a prior decision has clearly failed and needs triage, when time pressure demands rapid judgment with incomplete information, or when standard decision frameworks assume conditions that do not exist.

commands.name: foreman:trust-equation
commands.description: (foreman) Diagnoses and builds trust using Maister's Trust Equation: Trust = (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) / Self-Orientation. Evaluates each variable with evidence-based scoring and prescribes targeted improvements. Use when losing investor confidence, experiencing customer churn despite strong product, repairing damaged stakeholder relationships, preparing fundraising trust strategies, or auditing team trust dynamics.

commands.name: foreman:tuckman-team-stages
commands.description: (foreman) Diagnoses team development stage using Tuckman's five-phase model: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, and Adjourning. Prescribes stage-appropriate leadership actions and identifies progression barriers. Use when a new team is struggling to gel, conflict emerges after initial politeness, teams regress after adding new members, post-acquisition integration stalls, or leaders need to facilitate productive storming rather than suppress it.

commands.name: foreman:understanding-people
commands.description: (foreman) Applies modern personality-decoding and rapid-understanding techniques to entrepreneurial relationships. Covers the Enneagram as a superior alternative to Myers-Briggs for self-awareness and team communication, the discipline of getting anyone even when chemistry is absent, three-question rapid-understanding for first meetings, being interested rather than interesting, and addressing the pervasive loneliness that shapes professional interactions. Use when building cofounder relationships, conducting customer discovery, onboarding new hires, preparing for investor meetings, or diagnosing communication breakdowns within teams.

commands.name: foreman:vuca-framework
commands.description: (foreman) Classifies unpredictable environments into four distinct dimensions -- Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, and Ambiguity -- each requiring a different strategic response: Vision, Understanding, Clarity, and Agility respectively. Use when navigating regulatory grey zones, responding to sudden competitive disruption, reducing operational complexity during scaling, designing rapid experimentation programmes under ambiguity, or building organizational resilience.

commands.name: foreman:wanting-what-matters
commands.description: (foreman) Addresses the meta-question behind all decision-making: whether the entrepreneur is optimising for the right things. Covers the hedonic treadmill and 'happy-when' trap, Dickens's A Christmas Carol as a decision-making parable, what happiness research from the elderly consistently reveals, memento mori as a practical decision filter (the deathbed test), the regret-minimisation framework, and the distinction between ordinary moments and defining moments. Use when a founder suspects they are chasing metrics that do not produce satisfaction, when strategic priorities feel misaligned with personal values, when mortality awareness could sharpen decision-making, or when the question shifts from 'how do I get what I want?' to 'is what I want worth wanting?'

commands.name: foreman:what-is-a-story
commands.description: (foreman) Defines what qualifies as a genuine story versus an anecdote, romp, or report. Teaches the transformation requirement, the Dinner Test, and the personal-narrative principle. Use when a founder's pitch feels flat despite good content, when team presentations list facts without landing emotionally, when someone confuses a sequence of events with a compelling narrative, or when preparing any communication that must move people rather than merely inform them.

commands.name: foreman:win-win-negotiation
commands.description: (foreman) Prepares and conducts negotiations using Fisher and Ury's principled negotiation method from Getting to Yes. Applies four principles: separate people from problems, focus on interests not positions, generate options for mutual gain, and insist on objective criteria. Use when negotiating term sheets, structuring enterprise contracts, resolving co-founder equity disputes, preparing for acquisition discussions, or debriefing completed negotiations for improvement.

commands.name: foreman:writing-effective-emails
commands.description: (foreman) Provides a practical system for writing emails that get read, answered, and acted upon. Covers subject line craft, optimal length, formatting for scanning, tone calibration, CC/BCC etiquette, and when to choose a different medium entirely. Use when composing high-stakes emails to investors or clients, establishing email standards for a team, preparing sensitive written communications, or diagnosing why outreach emails receive poor response rates.

commands.name: foreman:writing-for-navigation
commands.description: (foreman) Provides a structural system for arranging written content so busy readers can find what matters within seconds. Covers BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front), visual hierarchy, headings as signposts, bullet point strategy, formatting discipline, and the map metaphor for document design. Use when structuring investor updates, redesigning internal communications, formatting product announcements, or diagnosing why well-written messages still fail to land.

commands.name: foreman:writing-for-response
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches how to write messages that convert reader understanding into reader action. Covers friction reduction, default design, the power of constrained choices, response-oriented formatting, and the 30-second response test. Use when crafting calls to action in emails or product copy, designing opt-in or enrolment flows, diagnosing low response rates on surveys or meeting requests, or building templates for action-oriented team communications.

commands.name: foreman:writing-memos-and-reports
commands.description: (foreman) Provides a systematic approach to structuring memos, reports, and business letters that inform decisions and drive action. Covers the Issue-Solution-Reason summary framework, the Who-Why-What-When-How planning chart, visual aids, three-audience writing, and business letter conventions. Use when drafting board memos, internal recommendations, market analysis reports, strategic proposals, client-facing letters, or any document longer than an email that must survive scrutiny from multiple readers.

commands.name: foreman:writing-performance-reviews
commands.description: (foreman) Guides the high-stakes process of writing performance appraisals that are specific, fair, legally defensible, and genuinely useful for employee development. Covers the seven evaluation dimensions (attitude, efficiency, human relations, judgment, knowledge, reliability, communication), the spectrum from superb to poor, the discipline of pairing evaluative language with concrete evidence, and the legal implications of imprecise writing. Use when preparing annual or quarterly reviews, designing performance evaluation templates, training first-time managers on review writing, or auditing existing review practices for fairness and consistency.

commands.name: foreman:writing-process
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches the MACJ writing process -- Madman, Architect, Carpenter, Judge -- a four-phase method for producing effective business documents by separating idea generation, organisation, drafting, and editing into distinct sequential tasks. Covers brainstorming, outlining in sets of three, speed writing, and disciplined revision. Use when facing writer's block, struggling to organise complex material, drafting reports or proposals, or when any business document feels overwhelming to start.

commands.name: foreman:writing-with-purpose
commands.description: (foreman) Teaches how purpose and audience analysis determine the form, tone, and content of every business communication. Applies the principle that the same facts, addressed to the same reader, produce radically different letters depending on the writer's objective. Use when drafting any business document, preparing investor updates, writing customer communications, crafting fundraising emails, or any situation where the writer is unsure what tone to strike or how to frame a message.

commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. """Click on the Hōrai case button and record the scroll glide, one rAF per sample.

    python click_scroll_probe.py URL [--scenario wait|fast] [--runs N] [--trace OUT.json]

wait: jump to #exempelcase, wait 1.5 s, click (the lead's original scenario).
fast: jump to #exempelcase, click 250 ms after the picker is reached (R7b).
Pass = arrived (within 2 px of the glide's end) inside 2.0 s, largest step
<= 60 px, and no frame longer than 100 ms during the first 2 s after the click.
--trace writes a CDP trace (headless, first run only) around the click.
Always headless.
"""
import sys, json, argparse
sys.path.insert(0, r"C:/Users/Anton L/anti-slop-design/tests/alunix-r8")
from showcase_probe import single_flight
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
ap.add_argument("url")
ap.add_argument("--scenario", choices=["wait", "fast"], default="wait")
ap.add_argument("--runs", type=int, default=1)
ap.add_argument("--trace")
a = ap.parse_args()
WAIT_MS = {"wait": 1500, "fast": 250}[a.scenario]
CATS = ["devtools.timeline", "disabled-by-default-devtools.timeline", "toplevel", "blink.user_timing",
        "v8.execute", "disabled-by-default-devtools.timeline.frame", "loading"]

single_flight()


def one(p, trace):
    b = p.chromium.launch(headless=True, channel="chromium", args=["--enable-gpu", "--ignore-gpu-blocklist", "--use-angle=d3d11"])
    try:
        pg = b.new_page(viewport={"width": 1440, "height": 900}); pg.goto(a.url, wait_until="load"); pg.wait_for_timeout(2000)
        pg.evaluate("""(()=>{window.__ev=[];const C=window.__CASES;for(const k in C){C[k].iframe.addEventListener('load',()=>__ev.push([k+':load',Math.round(performance.now())]));
          new MutationObserver(()=>__ev.push([k+':src',Math.round(performance.now())])).observe(C[k].iframe,{attributes:true,attributeFilter:['src']});}})()""")
        if trace: b.start_tracing(page=pg, categories=CATS)
        pg.evaluate("window.__jumpAt=performance.now();window.__lenis.scrollTo('#exempelcase',{immediate:true})"); pg.wait_for_timeout(WAIT_MS)
        tgt = pg.evaluate("(()=>{const r=document.getElementById('showcase').getBoundingClientRect();return Math.round(r.top+scrollY)})()")
        pg.evaluate("""window.__ys=[];let t0=performance.now();window.__clickAt=t0;(function f(){window.__ys.push([Math.round(performance.now()-t0),Math.round(scrollY)]); if(performance.now()-t0<3000) requestAnimationFrame(f)})()""")
        pg.evaluate("performance.mark('probe-click');document.querySelector('button.case-choice[data-case=horai]').click()")
        pg.wait_for_timeout(3200)
        ys, ev, t0, jump = pg.evaluate("[window.__ys, window.__ev, window.__clickAt, window.__jumpAt]")
        if trace:
            open(trace, "wb").write(b.stop_tracing())
    finally:
        b.close()
    ev = [(n, round(t - t0)) for n, t in ev]
    return ys, tgt, ev, round(t0 - jump)


res = []
with sync_playwright() as p:
    for r in range(a.runs):
        ys, tgt, ev, lag = one(p, a.trace if r == 0 else None)
        d = [ys[i+1][1]-ys[i][1] for i in range(len(ys)-1)]
        dt = [(ys[i+1][0], ys[i+1][0]-ys[i][0]) for i in range(len(ys)-1)]
        end = ys[-1][1]
        arrive = next((t for t, y in ys if abs(y - end) <= 2 and end - ys[0][1] > 100), None)
        maxstep = max(d) if d else 0
        maxframe = max((x for t, x in dt if t <= 2000), default=0)
        ok = arrive is not None and arrive <= 2000 and maxstep <= 60 and maxframe <= 100
        res.append(ok)
        print("run %d [%s, click %d ms after jump] %s | arrive %s ms | max step %d px | max frame %d ms (first 2 s) | y at 0/300/700/1400/2000 ms: %s | glide end %d (showcase top %d) | events: %s" % (
            r+1, a.scenario, lag, "PASS" if ok else "FAIL", arrive, maxstep, maxframe,
            [next((y for t, y in ys if t >= m), ys[-1][1]) for m in (0, 300, 700, 1400, 2000)], end, tgt, ev))
print("%s: %d/%d pass" % (a.scenario, sum(res), len(res)))
sys.exit(0 if all(res) else 1)

"""Summarize a CDP trace from click_scroll_probe.py --trace: every main-thread
task over 50 ms from 2 s before the click to 3 s after, with its biggest
child events (script by URL, parse, layout, decode, paint).

    python trace_summary.py TRACE.json
"""
import json, sys
from collections import defaultdict

ev = json.load(open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"))
ev = ev["traceEvents"] if isinstance(ev, dict) else ev
names = {(e["pid"], e["tid"]): e["args"]["name"] for e in ev if e.get("name") == "thread_name"}
click = next(e["ts"] for e in ev if e.get("name") == "probe-click")
main = [(pid, tid) for (pid, tid), n in names.items() if n == "CrRendererMain"]
KEEP = {"EvaluateScript", "FunctionCall", "ParseHTML", "Layout", "UpdateLayoutTree", "Paint", "Decode Image",
        "ImageDecodeTask", "ParseAuthorStyleSheet", "TimerFire", "FireAnimationFrame", "EventDispatch",
        "v8.compile", "V8.CompileCode", "PrePaint", "Commit", "UpdateLayerTree", "RasterTask", "HitTest",
        "ScheduleStyleRecalculation", "FireIdleCallback", "v8.run", "CompileScript", "XHRLoad"}


def label(e):
    d = e.get("args", {}).get("data", {}) or e.get("args", {}).get("beginData", {}) or {}
    x = d.get("url") or d.get("type") or d.get("functionName") or ""
    return e["name"] + (" " + x.split("/")[-1][:60] if x else "")


for pid, tid in main:
    th = [e for e in ev if e.get("pid") == pid and e.get("tid") == tid and e.get("ph") == "X" and "dur" in e]
    tasks = [e for e in th if e["name"] in ("RunTask", "ThreadControllerImpl::RunTask") and e["dur"] > 50000
             and -2e6 < e["ts"] - click < 3e6]
    if not tasks:
        continue
    print("== main thread pid %s tid %s: %d tasks > 50 ms" % (pid, tid, len(tasks)))
    for t in tasks:
        kids = defaultdict(float)
        for e in th:
            if e["name"] in KEEP and t["ts"] <= e["ts"] < t["ts"] + t["dur"]:
                kids[label(e)] += e["dur"] / 1000
        top = sorted(kids.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:7]
        print("  t=%+6d ms  %4d ms  " % ((t["ts"] - click) / 1000, t["dur"] / 1000) + "; ".join("%s %.0f" % kv for kv in top))

import json,sys
from collections import defaultdict
ev=json.load(open(sys.argv[1],encoding="utf-8")); ev=ev["traceEvents"] if isinstance(ev,dict) else ev
names={(e["pid"],e["tid"]):e["args"]["name"] for e in ev if e.get("name")=="thread_name"}
click=next(e["ts"] for e in ev if e.get("name")=="probe-click")
agg=defaultdict(float); cnt=defaultdict(int); big=[]
for e in ev:
    if e.get("ph")!="X" or "dur" not in e: continue
    r=(e["ts"]-click)/1000
    if not (0<=r<=2000): continue
    th=names.get((e["pid"],e["tid"]),"?")
    if e["name"] in ("ImageDecodeTask","Decode Image","RasterTask","GPUTask","Decode LazyPixelRef","ImageFrameGenerator::decode","DecodeAndScale","TileManager::RunTasks","RasterDecoderImpl::DoEndRasterCHROMIUM","CommandBufferStub::OnAsyncFlush","ThreadPool_RunTask","Scheduler::RunTask"):

        if e["dur"]>80000: big.append((round(r),round(e["dur"]/1000),th,e["name"],str(e.get("args"))[:140]))
for k,v in sorted(agg.items(),key=lambda kv:-kv[1])[:14]: print("%-45s %-35s %6.0f ms  n=%d"%(k[0],k[1],v,cnt[k]))
print("-- single events > 80 ms"); [print(b) for b in sorted(big)[:25]]
# rAF gaps on main
m=[e["ts"] for e in ev if e.get("name")=="FireAnimationFrame" and names.get((e["pid"],e["tid"]))=="CrRendererMain" and 0<=e["ts"]-click<=2e6]
m=sorted(set(m)); gaps=[(round((m[i]-click)/1000),round((m[i+1]-m[i])/1000)) for i in range(len(m)-1) if m[i+1]-m[i]>80000]
print("-- rAF gaps > 80 ms (start, len):",gaps)
EOF

1	# Chain discipline
2	
3	**Resident. Not routed.** This file loads with `SKILL.md` and is read by every
4	builder, every reviewer and every orchestrator in this chain, on every job.
5	It is the one document that is about *us* rather than about the page.
6	
7	It exists because of a five-day run (Alunix V3d, 2026-09-15 → 09-20) that spent
8	**37 build rounds on 10 orders**, cost $24 for the last round alone, and ended
9	with the owner's verdict:
10	
11	> *"resten av ändringarna motsvarade inte riktigt heller mina förväntningar även
12	> om de utfördes på papper."*
13	> — Anton, 2026-09-20
14	
15	Nothing in that run failed for lack of craft. Every ordered point was built and
16	rendered. It failed because **the chain lied to itself five times and believed
17	each lie** — and every lie became a build round before anyone caught it. The
18	rules below are those five lies and their fixes, plus the four method changes
19	that came out of the same run.
20	
21	**The rule everything else serves:** *a measurement you have not proven against
22	a known-broken case is not a measurement, it is a guess with a number on it.*
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1 · Measurement
27	
28	### M1 · Register every custom property before you read it
29	
30	`getPropertyValue('--tx')` on an **unregistered** custom property returns the
31	token stream — `clamp(0,calc((0.3214 - 0.2258) / 0.1613),1)` — not a number.
32	`parseFloat` on that is `NaN`, and `NaN` silently compares as `0` in every filter
33	and every `if`.
34	
35	**What it cost:** the `--slit-p` filter was inert through round 18 *and* through
36	two of Astra's review passes without anyone noticing. It then convinced the lead
37	that a colour draw had not started when `--tx` was in fact `0.59`, and that
38	false reading was written up as a finding before it was caught.
39	
40	**The rule.** Every numeric custom property that any script, probe or reviewer
41	reads must be declared:
42	
43	```css
44	@property --tx     { syntax: '<number>'; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }
45	@property --slit-p { syntax: '<number>'; inherits: true; initial-value: 0; }
46	```
47	
48	Declare it when the property is created, not when a measurement fails. If you
49	are reading a property that is not declared, **that is the finding** — declare
50	it first, then measure.
51	
52	**The check that proves the check:** run `parseFloat(getComputedStyle(el)
53	.getPropertyValue('--tx'))` against the *current, undeclared* state first. It
54	must return `NaN`. A version of this check that returns a number against both a
55	declared and an undeclared property is measuring nothing.
56	
57	### M2 · Never judge an act in a preview mode
58	
59	A `?preview=<name>` mode is a convenience that lands the page at a scroll
60	position. It is **not** evidence that the act renders correctly at that
61	position, and it drifts silently the moment the act's scroll window changes.
62	
63	**What it cost:** when plan 067 recomputed the act's window from hard-coded
64	numbers to calculated ones, every preview mode kept aiming at the old window. At
65	`tes-till-ritning-3` the sheet sat **1329 px below the viewport**. Every review
66	that had used the preview modes since — Astra's included — had been judging the
67	wrong scroll position.
68	
69	**The rule.** Before you judge an act from a preview mode, prove the mode lands
70	where it claims: read the element's bounding box against the viewport in that
71	mode and assert the overlap you expect. Failing that, **measure in real wheel
72	scroll** — `mouse.wheel`, 20 px steps, both directions — and say in your report
73	which method you used.
74	
75	### M3 · Every geometric check proves itself against a broken variant first
76	
77	Run each structural check **against a deliberately broken build** before you run
78	it against the real one. A check that returns green against both a broken and a
79	correct page measures nothing, and it will do so quietly, forever.
80	
81	**What it cost:** it has happened three times in this project. Astra discarded
82	two of her own probe versions in r21 for exactly this reason, and rebuilt her
83	column probe in r22 after a false negative.
84	
85	**The rule.** Every check ships with its injected fault, named in the report:
86	*"`.chapter-plate{clip-path:none;height:+900px}` → N hits, clean build → 0."*
87	A check reported without its broken-case value is not evidence and may not be
88	cited as one.
89	
90	---
91	
92	## 2 · Verification
93	
94	### V1 · A review surface never caches
95	
96	**What it cost:** `board.py` sent only `Last-Modified`, no cache headers. Chrome
97	applied heuristic freshness and served a previous round without revalidating.
98	The owner reviewed stale code **at least twice**, concluded nothing had been
99	built, and had to ask *"är det ens något gjort?"* — a reasonable conclusion from
100	what he was actually looking at.
101	
102	Fixed in `scripts/board.py` (`Cache-Control: no-store, must-revalidate`). The
103	rule outlives the fix: **any surface a human uses to judge work must be
104	uncacheable, and must say so in a header, not in a hope.**
105	
106	If you are ever handed a review surface and cannot state its cache behaviour,
107	assume it is lying to you until you have force-reloaded it once.
108	
109	### V2 · Verify in the render, not in the bytes
110	
111	**What it cost:** the lead grepped the served cell over HTTP, found the change,
112	and reported *"ändringarna finns"* — while the owner was looking at a page that
113	did not have it. Bytes on a server prove nothing about what a browser paints.
114	
115	**The rule.** "It is in the file" is not a verification. "It is in the response
116	body" is not a verification. The verification is **a rendered image of the page
117	the human will actually open**, read as an image, by the person making the claim.
118	When the two disagree, the render wins, and the discrepancy is itself the finding.
119	
120	---
121	
122	## 3 · Orchestration
123	
124	### O1 · Run Codex directly, never through a wrapper agent
125	
126	`Agent(codex-review)` cost **305,000 Opus tokens per round**. Inside that, the
127	actual Codex call was **one request, 24 images in, 6.3 kB of text out** — billed
128	to the OpenAI quota, not to ours. The other ~300k was an Opus subagent
129	re-doing the measurement work before asking the question.
130	
131	**The rule.** Drive `codex exec` from the shell. `scripts/astra.py` takes a
132	prompt file, a screenshot glob and an output path, and reads the answer back.
133	Screenshots come from a capture script; the prompt comes from you; the verdict
134	costs almost nothing.
135	
136	**What you must NOT drop along with the wrapper.** The wrapper verified every
137	Codex finding against the file and the pixels before releasing it. In r21, three
138	of Codex's four findings fell to that check. **The verification step is
139	mandatory and it is now yours.** A Codex verdict is a draft, never a finding.
140	
141	`astra.py` refuses two failure modes by construction and both matter: an empty
142	response is an **error**, not "no findings"; and more than ~28 images produces
143	sludge, so the selection must be narrowed rather than padded.
144	
145	### O2 · A plan that is not on disk does not exist
146	
147	**What it cost:** an architect subagent reported a complete plan **three times**
148	without being able to save it, and said so only when asked for the files
149	directly. A builder was nearly dispatched against a plan that was never written.
150	
151	**The rule.** `subagent_type: Plan` is read-only. Before any builder is
152	dispatched, **`Read` the plan file from disk and confirm it is the plan you
153	think it is.** A plan reported in a message is a draft. The artifact is the file.
154	
155	Same rule for reference baselines, målbilder and captured screenshots: if the
156	path cannot be opened right now, it is not an input.
157	
158	---
159	
160	## 4 · Review
161	
162	### R1 · Aesthetic review is a sanctioned mode
163	
164	This is the single largest method gain in the run, and it was nearly lost.
165	
166	`agents/codex-review.md` was written for code and measurements. In r23 it was
167	instead given the mandate *"varför är detta fult, och vad skulle göra det
168	vackert"*, with the customer's rejection treated as correct by definition and the
169	reviewer instructed to find **what it had missed**. The result was the best
170	review in the project's history. Astra wrote, in plain terms:
171	
172	> *"Jag mätte att den klippta rektangeln äger 44 % av viewporten och kallade det
173	> 'en hel yta som förändras'. Jag mätte formens area och tog den för närvaro."*
174	
175	...and then produced a direction a builder could draw from, rather than a defect
176	list.
177	
178	**The rule.** When the owner rejects work that passed every gate, the failure is
179	not in the gates — it is that no one was asked the aesthetic question. Dispatch
180	Astra in **`mode: aesthetic`**, with these framings:
181	
182	- The customer has already judged it and the customer is right by definition.
183	  Your job is not to defend the work; it is to find what you failed to see.
184	- Name *why* it is ugly in the terms of form — area, weight, rhythm, contrast,
185	  what owns the viewport — not in adjectives.
186	- Weight the answer in `fidelity` and `ceiling`. An aesthetic pass whose output
187	  is a defect list has failed at its one job.
188	
189	**What this does not license.** An aesthetic pass may not re-choose the palette,
190	the type or the direction — that is still a Step 2 decision and still a
191	gate-order violation. It judges how well the *committed* direction is executed,
192	and where the execution reads as empty. The distinction is exact: **"this is
193	badly executed against its own intent" is a finding; "it would look better as
194	something else" is not.**
195	
196	### R2 · A rule in prose needs a mechanical test
197	
198	**What it cost:** F-018 (*the page never narrates itself*) was written into
199	`FEEDBACK.md`, `anti-patterns.md`, `gates.md`, `copy-gate.md` and
200	`production-tells.md` — and then broken by the very next sentence the chain
201	delivered:
202	
203	> *"Vi har ingen husstil. Formen kommer ur verksamheten, och därför valde vi de
204	> två projekt som ligger längst ifrån varandra."*
205	
206	New words, same posture. The sentence explains **the page's own selection** to
207	the reader; nobody asked why those two examples are on the page. It passed the
208	scanner because the rule was written for microtext and this was set in body size.
209	
210	**The rule.** Every copy rule that names a *shape* rather than a word gets a
211	mechanical check, or it will be broken by the next fluent paragraph. F-018's
212	check is `scripts/self_reference_scan.py`: it flags every sentence whose subject
213	is the page, the section, the example or the selection. Run it on the rendered
214	copy, and run it against the sentence above first — it must flag it.
215	
216	A prose rule with no test is a preference, and preferences lose to fluency.
217	
218	---
219	
220	## 5 · The round ladder
221	
222	The five rules above stop the chain lying. This one stops the spiral.
223	
224	**37 rounds for 10 orders** was not a speed problem. It was that **no round was
225	ever allowed to finish before the next one started.** Round 23 built nine ordered
226	points and never ran its own § Verification; the nine were then judged
227	"executed on paper" and the level not reached, which is the only verdict possible
228	when nobody checked.
229	
230	**The ladder, in order, no skipping:**
231	
232	1. **Plan on disk** (O2). Read it before dispatching.
233	2. **Build one round.**
234	3. **Verify that round completely** — its own plan's § Verification, all of it,
235	   not the parts that fit the remaining budget. Disk space, quota and time are
236	   not verification exemptions; if they run out, the round is **incomplete**, and
237	   that is what gets reported.
238	4. **Only then** does the next round start.
239	
240	**A round may not be retro-fitted.** If round N's verification reveals a fault,
241	the fix is round N+1 — never a silent edit folded into round N+2's build.
242	
243	**And the reporting rule that follows from all of it:** a round whose images
244	nobody has looked at has not been verified, whatever the log says. Do not report
245	a build as done on the strength of a green exit code. The builder reporting
246	"grinden grön" while the lead's own reading found a new fault is not a rare
247	event — it happened in r20 and r22 of this run.
248	
249	---
250	
251	## 6 · Where these rules are enforced
252	
253	| Rule | Written into | Mechanised by |
254	|---|---|---|
255	| M1 register properties | this file | the `@property` block; check returns `NaN` on undeclared |
256	| M2 preview modes | this file | bounding-box assertion, or wheel scroll |
257	| M3 broken-variant first | this file · `design-verify` | every probe ships its injected fault |
258	| V1 no caching | this file | `scripts/board.py` `Cache-Control` |
259	| V2 render not bytes | this file · `agents/design-critic.md` | the review contract's `recapture` disposition |
260	| O1 Codex direct | this file · `agents/codex-review.md` | `scripts/astra.py` |
261	| O2 plan on disk | this file | `Read` the file before dispatch |
262	| R1 aesthetic mode | this file · `agents/codex-review.md` | `mode: aesthetic` in the dispatch |
263	| R2 rule needs a test | this file · `copy-gate.md` | `scripts/self_reference_scan.py` |
264	
265	**The one-line version, if you keep only one:** *the customer's rejection is
266	evidence, the chain's own measurement is a claim, and an unverified round is not
267	finished — it is unfinished, and says so.*
268

**The rule.** "It is in the file" is not a verification. "It is in the response
body" is not a verification. The verification is **a rendered image of the page
the human will actually open**, read as an image, by the person making the claim.
When the two disagree, the render wins, and the discrepancy is itself the finding.

---

## 3 · Orchestration

### O1 · Run Codex directly, never through a wrapper agent

`Agent(codex-review)` cost **305,000 Opus tokens per round**. Inside that, the
actual Codex call was **one request, 24 images in, 6.3 kB of text out** — billed
to the OpenAI quota, not to ours. The other ~300k was an Opus subagent
re-doing the measurement work before asking the question.

**The rule.** Drive `codex exec` from the shell. `scripts/astra.py` takes a
prompt file, a screenshot glob and an output path, and reads the answer back.
Screenshots come from a capture script; the prompt comes from you; the verdict
costs almost nothing.

**What you must NOT drop along with the wrapper.** The wrapper verified every
Codex finding against the file and the pixels before releasing it. In r21, three
of Codex's four findings fell to that check. **The verification step is
mandatory and it is now yours.** A Codex verdict is a draft, never a finding.

`astra.py` refuses two failure modes by construction and both matter: an empty
response is an **error**, not "no findings"; and more than ~28 images produces
sludge, so the selection must be narrowed rather than padded.

### O2 · A plan that is not on disk does not exist

**What it cost:** an architect subagent reported a complete plan **three times**
without being able to save it, and said so only when asked for the files
directly. A builder was nearly dispatched against a plan that was never written.

**The rule.** `subagent_type: Plan` is read-only. Before any builder is
dispatched, **`Read` the plan file from disk and confirm it is the plan you
think it is.** A plan reported in a message is a draft. The artifact is the file.

Same rule for reference baselines, målbilder and captured screenshots: if the
path cannot be opened right now, it is not an input.

---

## 4 · Review

### R1 · Aesthetic review is a sanctioned mode

This is the single largest method gain in the run, and it was nearly lost.

`agents/codex-review.md` was written for code and measurements. In r23 it was
instead given the mandate *"varför är detta fult, och vad skulle göra det
vackert"*, with the customer's rejection treated as correct by definition and the
reviewer instructed to find **what it had missed**. The result was the best
review in the project's history. Astra wrote, in plain terms:

> *"Jag mätte att den klippta rektangeln äger 44 % av viewporten och kallade det
> 'en hel yta som förändras'. Jag mätte formens area och tog den för närvaro."*

...and then produced a direction a builder could draw from, rather than a defect
list.

**The rule.** When the owner rejects work that passed every gate, the failure is
not in the gates — it is that no one was asked the aesthetic question. Dispatch
Astra in **`mode: aesthetic`**, with these framings:

- The customer has already judged it and the customer is right by definition.
  Your job is not to defend the work; it is to find what you failed to see.
- Name *why* it is ugly in the terms of form — area, weight, rhythm, contrast,
  what owns the viewport — not in adjectives.
- Weight the answer in `fidelity` and `ceiling`. An aesthetic pass whose output
  is a defect list has failed at its one job.

**What this does not license.** An aesthetic pass may not re-choose the palette,
the type or the direction — that is still a Step 2 decision and still a
gate-order violation. It judges how well the *committed* direction is executed,
and where the execution reads as empty. The distinction is exact: **"this is
badly executed against its own intent" is a finding; "it would look better as
something else" is not.**

### R2 · A rule in prose needs a mechanical test

**What it cost:** F-018 (*the page never narrates itself*) was written into
`FEEDBACK.md`, `anti-patterns.md`, `gates.md`, `copy-gate.md` and
`production-tells.md` — and then broken by the very next sentence the chain
delivered:

> *"Vi har ingen husstil. Formen kommer ur verksamheten, och därför valde vi de
> två projekt som ligger längst ifrån varandra."*

New words, same posture. The sentence explains **the page's own selection** to
the reader; nobody asked why those two examples are on the page. It passed the
scanner because the rule was written for microtext and this was set in body size.

**The rule.** Every copy rule that names a *shape* rather than a word gets a
mechanical check, or it will be broken by the next fluent paragraph. F-018's
check is `scripts/self_reference_scan.py`: it flags every sentence whose subject
is the page, the section, the example or the selection. Run it on the rendered
copy, and run it against the sentence above first — it must flag it.

A prose rule with no test is a preference, and preferences lose to fluency.

---

## 5 · The round ladder

The five rules above stop the chain lying. This one stops the spiral.

**37 rounds for 10 orders** was not a speed problem. It was that **no round was
ever allowed to finish before the next one started.** Round 23 built nine ordered
points and never ran its own § Verification; the nine were then judged
"executed on paper" and the level not reached, which is the only verdict possible
when nobody checked.

**The ladder, in order, no skipping:**

1. **Plan on disk** (O2). Read it before dispatching.
2. **Build one round.**
3. **Verify that round completely** — its own plan's § Verification, all of it,
   not the parts that fit the remaining budget. Disk space, quota and time are
   not verification exemptions; if they run out, the round is **incomplete**, and
   that is what gets reported.
4. **Only then** does the next round start.

**A round may not be retro-fitted.** If round N's verification reveals a fault,
the fix is round N+1 — never a silent edit folded into round N+2's build.

**And the reporting rule that follows from all of it:** a round whose images
nobody has looked at has not been verified, whatever the log says. Do not report
a build as done on the strength of a green exit code. The builder reporting
"grinden grön" while the lead's own reading found a new fault is not a rare
event — it happened in r20 and r22 of this run.

---

## 6 · Where these rules are enforced

| Rule | Written into | Mechanised by |
|---|---|---|
| M1 register properties | this file | the `@property` block; check returns `NaN` on undeclared |
| M2 preview modes | this file | bounding-box assertion, or wheel scroll |
| M3 broken-variant first | this file · `design-verify` | every probe ships its injected fault |
| V1 no caching | this file | `scripts/board.py` `Cache-Control` |
| V2 render not bytes | this file · `agents/design-critic.md` | the review contract's `recapture` disposition |
| O1 Codex direct | this file · `agents/codex-review.md` | `scripts/astra.py` |
| O2 plan on disk | this file | `Read` the file before dispatch |
| R1 aesthetic mode | this file · `agents/codex-review.md` | `mode: aesthetic` in the dispatch |
| R2 rule needs a test | this file · `copy-gate.md` | `scripts/self_reference_scan.py` |

**The one-line version, if you keep only one:** *the customer's rejection is
evidence, the chain's own measurement is a claim, and an unverified round is not
finished — it is unfinished, and says so.*

138	
139	### Modernisation levers, in priority order
140	
141	Apply in order; stop when the brief is satisfied.
142	
143	1. **Typography refresh** — biggest visual lift per unit of risk.
144	2. **Spacing and rhythm** — section padding, vertical rhythm.
145	3. **Colour recalibration** — desaturate, unify neutrals, keep the brand accent.
146	4. **Motion layer** — micro-interactions on existing components.
147	5. **Hero and key-section recomposition** — restructure top-of-funnel.
148	6. **Full block replacement** — only when a block is unsalvageable.
149	
150	Decision rule: if IA, content, and SEO are sound, take **targeted evolution** (levers 1–4) — roughly 70% of the value at 40% of the risk. Go to full redesign only when the visual debt is structural (broken IA, no design system, broken mobile). If the brand itself is changing, that is greenfield.
151

153	
154	Never modify without explicit approval:
155	
156	- URL structure and route slugs
157	- Primary nav labels
158	- Form field names or order (breaks analytics and autofill)
159	- Brand logo or wordmark
160	- Existing legal, consent, or cookie copy
161	
162	---
163

165	
166	Claude Design's **inline-styles-only** rule is deliberately **not** ported. 1	# Motion smoothness — why a page that renders correctly can still look cheap
2	
3	Anton, r7 (FEEDBACK.md F-012): *"scrolleffekten renderade som den skulle, men det såg
4	hackigt och billigt gjort ut."* The measured answer is F-013. Read this before writing
5	any scroll-driven motion, and read it again before "fixing" motion that someone has
6	called janky — because **two different faults produce that same sentence**, and the cure
7	for one does nothing for the other.
8	
9	## The two faults
10	
11	| | The value steps | The page drops frames |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| What you see | Motion advances in visible notches | Motion stutters and lags the hand |
14	| What the clock says | 60 fps, nothing wrong | frame p95 well over 20 ms |
15	| Where it comes from | A raw scroll value written 1:1 | Too much work per frame |
16	| What fixes it | Damp the value (`--sc-ps`) | Cut the work (`performance.md`) |
17	
18	Measure both before changing anything: `scripts/motion_probe.py` reports frame time and
19	value continuity in one run. Guessing which fault you have is how a session spends an
20	afternoon smoothing something that was never stepping.
21	
22	## Fault 1 — the raw value
23	
24	`scrollcraft.js` damps exactly two things: the video playhead (lerp 0.18, deadband,
25	seek coalescing) and the pointer devices `tilt` / `magnet`. Its own docstring explains
26	why: *"wheel events do not arrive at a constant rate and a 1:1 write reproduces every
27	gap in them."*
28	
29	That reasoning is right, and the engine does not apply it to `--sc-p`. Everything
30	`read()` writes — `--sc-p` itself, cue opacity, parallax, pan, kinetic units,
31	`clip-path`, drift — is written 1:1 from raw scroll position, on the scroll event
32	behind a one-frame rAF guard. On a mouse wheel the value stands still between notches
33	and then jumps.
34	
35	Two things make it worse:
36	
37	- **`--sc-p` is an unregistered custom property.** To CSS it is a string, so it never
38	  interpolates, and no `@property` registration exists anywhere in the engine.
39	- **`scrollcraft.css` sets `transition: none`** on `[data-sc-cue]` and `[data-sc-copy]`
40	  once `.sc-ready` lands. That is deliberate — JS owns the value — but it means nothing
41	  bridges the gap between two writes.
42	
43	**F-011 did not cause this.** `var reduce = false` turned the playhead lerp *on*
44	(rate 1.0 → 0.18). `reduce` gates ten sites in the engine and every one is a disable
45	branch. The stepping is architectural and predates the override.
46	
47	### The rule
48	
49	> **Bespoke motion reads `--sc-ps`, never raw `--sc-p`, whenever it drives something the
50	> eye sees move** — `transform`, `object-position`, `clip-path`, `mask-position`,
51	> `background-position`. Cue opacity may read `--sc-p`.
52	
53	`--sc-ps` is published by `scripts/scroll/sc-smooth.js`, copied in beside the engine and
54	loaded after it. The engine is never edited (`scroll/NOTE.md`: copy, never edit). The
55	shim lerps at 0.16 per frame with a 0.0005 deadband, registers `--sc-ps` as a real
56	`<number>` so CSS can interpolate it, stops its own rAF loop when nothing is moving, and
57	sets `will-change` **only while an act is actually in motion** — correcting the engine
58	CSS's seven class-level promotions, which `motion.md` § Bans forbids.
59	
60	A page's own rAF painters (`paintHeroPool`, `paintMotion`, a word scrub) read `--sc-ps`
61	too. `?preview=` modes set `window.__scFreezeMotion = true`, and the shim then tracks the
62	raw value exactly so a screenshot shows the formed state, not a lerp in flight.
63	
64	Measured, same motion, same wheel cadence (`tests/motion/`):
65	
66	| | frame p95 | staircase | largest single-frame step |
67	|---|---|---|---|
68	| `staircase.html` (raw `--sc-p` → `rotateY`) | 16.7 ms | 18 | 5.6 % |
69	| `smooth.html` (lerped) | 16.7 ms | **0** | **1.4 %** |
70	
71	The frame clock is identical in both. The difference is entirely in the value.
72	
73	## Fault 2 — the page is genuinely slow
74	
75	Damping a value on a page that cannot hold 60 fps just makes a smooth curve arrive late.
76	V3b, measured 2026-09-08 with no CPU throttling at all: frame p95 49.9 ms, 62 frames over
77	33 ms, 4.9 MB transferred, 19 font files, 17 long tasks during scroll, four elements with
78	a resting `will-change`. See `performance.md` for the budget and `scripts/perf_probe.py`
79	for the measurement.
80	
81	## Pace — the third thing people call "not smooth"
82	
83	From upstream scroll-craft's `worldflight.md` § 7c, the only place in the corpus where
84	someone diagnosed the complaint to root cause: *"Two separate faults get described as
85	'it doesn't feel smooth', and only one of them is smoothing."*
86	
87	- **Inconsistent pace is the worse one.** Across a multi-act or multi-leg sequence,
88	  `rate = weight / seconds` must hold within a few percent. On the `orrery` build it
89	  varied 36 % across ten legs and the owner's word for it was "not smooth"; evened to
90	  6 %, the same footage read as one continuous move.
91	- **Too fast reads as cheap.** For a fly-through, 0.21–0.22 vh per second of film is the
92	  floor. The per-8-seconds guardrail is a dead-scroll floor, not a taste target.
93	- **Damping and weights fix different halves.** *"The damping is what removes wheel
94	  judder; the weights are what remove the surging."* For a worldflight use
95	  `data-sc-lerp` **0.12**, not the 0.18 default, and widen `data-sc-seam` to ~0.16.
96	
97	`motion_probe.py` reports `max_step` per act, so an act that surges relative to its
98	neighbours shows up as a spread across runs rather than as a feeling. Full port, with
99	the weight arithmetic and the worldflight knob values: [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md).
100	
101	## The bar
102	
103	A signature act is not finished until, at 4× CPU throttling:
104	
105	- `staircase = 0`
106	- `max_step ≤ 3 %` of the value's own range **on the damped playhead `--sc-ps`**; on a
107	  derived track (`transform`, `clip-path`, …) it is reported, not gated — a smoothstepped
108	  value peaks at ~4.4 % per frame by its own derivative, and `staircase` is the number
109	  that catches a step there (r8 R2: V3c's flip at 4.12 %, staircase 0, was correct)
110	- frame p95 ≤ 20 ms, zero frames over 33 ms
111	- both scroll directions measured, not just downward
112	- measured in a quiet window: run `tests/motion/smooth.html` first as a control; if the
113	  control shows any frame over 33 ms, the host is busy and the page's numbers are noise
114	
115	## What the harness still cannot tell you
116	
117	Upstream's `verify.md` says it plainly: *"Whether the motion is smooth. Contiguous frames
118	prove the clip advances; they do not prove it advances evenly."* `motion_probe.py` closes
119	most of that gap and does not close all of it. Watch the contact sheet for a move that
120	lurches, reverses, or stalls in the middle, and watch the sparkline the probe writes: a
121	curve with a flat shoulder is an act that stops dead mid-travel, which no single number
122	reports.
123	
124	One known, accepted inconsistency: `scripts/scroll/scrollcraft.css` line 98 still carries
125	`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { html { scroll-behavior: auto } }`. It only
126	disables smooth anchor jumping and touches no act, and the engine is never edited, so it
127	stays — documented here rather than silently tolerated.
128	
129	## Related
130	
131	[`scroll/devices.md`](scroll/devices.md) · [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md) ·
132	[`performance.md`](performance.md) ·
133	[`motion.md`](motion.md) · `scripts/motion_probe.py` · `scripts/scroll/sc-smooth.js` ·
134	FEEDBACK.md F-011, F-012, F-013.

# Motion smoothness — why a page that renders correctly can still look cheap

Anton, r7 (FEEDBACK.md F-012): *"scrolleffekten renderade som den skulle, men det såg
hackigt och billigt gjort ut."* The measured answer is F-013. Read this before writing
any scroll-driven motion, and read it again before "fixing" motion that someone has
called janky — because **two different faults produce that same sentence**, and the cure
for one does nothing for the other.

## The two faults

| | The value steps | The page drops frames |
|---|---|---|
| What you see | Motion advances in visible notches | Motion stutters and lags the hand |
| What the clock says | 60 fps, nothing wrong | frame p95 well over 20 ms |
| Where it comes from | A raw scroll value written 1:1 | Too much work per frame |
| What fixes it | Damp the value (`--sc-ps`) | Cut the work (`performance.md`) |

Measure both before changing anything: `scripts/motion_probe.py` reports frame time and
value continuity in one run. Guessing which fault you have is how a session spends an
afternoon smoothing something that was never stepping.

## Fault 1 — the raw value

`scrollcraft.js` damps exactly two things: the video playhead (lerp 0.18, deadband,
seek coalescing) and the pointer devices `tilt` / `magnet`. Its own docstring explains
why: *"wheel events do not arrive at a constant rate and a 1:1 write reproduces every
gap in them."*

That reasoning is right, and the engine does not apply it to `--sc-p`. Everything
`read()` writes — `--sc-p` itself, cue opacity, parallax, pan, kinetic units,
`clip-path`, drift — is written 1:1 from raw scroll position, on the scroll event
behind a one-frame rAF guard. On a mouse wheel the value stands still between notches
and then jumps.

Two things make it worse:

- **`--sc-p` is an unregistered custom property.** To CSS it is a string, so it never
  interpolates, and no `@property` registration exists anywhere in the engine.
- **`scrollcraft.css` sets `transition: none`** on `[data-sc-cue]` and `[data-sc-copy]`
  once `.sc-ready` lands. That is deliberate — JS owns the value — but it means nothing
  bridges the gap between two writes.

**F-011 did not cause this.** `var reduce = false` turned the playhead lerp *on*
(rate 1.0 → 0.18). `reduce` gates ten sites in the engine and every one is a disable
branch. The stepping is architectural and predates the override.

### The rule

> **Bespoke motion reads `--sc-ps`, never raw `--sc-p`, whenever it drives something the
> eye sees move** — `transform`, `object-position`, `clip-path`, `mask-position`,
> `background-position`. Cue opacity may read `--sc-p`.

`--sc-ps` is published by `scripts/scroll/sc-smooth.js`, copied in beside the engine and
loaded after it. The engine is never edited (`scroll/NOTE.md`: copy, never edit). The
shim lerps at 0.16 per frame with a 0.0005 deadband, registers `--sc-ps` as a real
`<number>` so CSS can interpolate it, stops its own rAF loop when nothing is moving, and
sets `will-change` **only while an act is actually in motion** — correcting the engine
CSS's seven class-level promotions, which `motion.md` § Bans forbids.

A page's own rAF painters (`paintHeroPool`, `paintMotion`, a word scrub) read `--sc-ps`
too. `?preview=` modes set `window.__scFreezeMotion = true`, and the shim then tracks the
raw value exactly so a screenshot shows the formed state, not a lerp in flight.

Measured, same motion, same wheel cadence (`tests/motion/`):

| | frame p95 | staircase | largest single-frame step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `staircase.html` (raw `--sc-p` → `rotateY`) | 16.7 ms | 18 | 5.6 % |
| `smooth.html` (lerped) | 16.7 ms | **0** | **1.4 %** |

The frame clock is identical in both. The difference is entirely in the value.

## Fault 2 — the page is genuinely slow

Damping a value on a page that cannot hold 60 fps just makes a smooth curve arrive late.
V3b, measured 2026-09-08 with no CPU throttling at all: frame p95 49.9 ms, 62 frames over
33 ms, 4.9 MB transferred, 19 font files, 17 long tasks during scroll, four elements with
a resting `will-change`. See `performance.md` for the budget and `scripts/perf_probe.py`
for the measurement.

## Pace — the third thing people call "not smooth"

From upstream scroll-craft's `worldflight.md` § 7c, the only place in the corpus where
someone diagnosed the complaint to root cause: *"Two separate faults get described as
'it doesn't feel smooth', and only one of them is smoothing."*

- **Inconsistent pace is the worse one.** Across a multi-act or multi-leg sequence,
  `rate = weight / seconds` must hold within a few percent. On the `orrery` build it
  varied 36 % across ten legs and the owner's word for it was "not smooth"; evened to
  6 %, the same footage read as one continuous move.
- **Too fast reads as cheap.** For a fly-through, 0.21–0.22 vh per second of film is the
  floor. The per-8-seconds guardrail is a dead-scroll floor, not a taste target.
- **Damping and weights fix different halves.** *"The damping is what removes wheel
  judder; the weights are what remove the surging."* For a worldflight use
  `data-sc-lerp` **0.12**, not the 0.18 default, and widen `data-sc-seam` to ~0.16.

`motion_probe.py` reports `max_step` per act, so an act that surges relative to its
neighbours shows up as a spread across runs rather than as a feeling. Full port, with
the weight arithmetic and the worldflight knob values: [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md).

## The bar

A signature act is not finished until, at 4× CPU throttling:

- `staircase = 0`
- `max_step ≤ 3 %` of the value's own range **on the damped playhead `--sc-ps`**; on a
  derived track (`transform`, `clip-path`, …) it is reported, not gated — a smoothstepped
  value peaks at ~4.4 % per frame by its own derivative, and `staircase` is the number
  that catches a step there (r8 R2: V3c's flip at 4.12 %, staircase 0, was correct)
- frame p95 ≤ 20 ms, zero frames over 33 ms
- both scroll directions measured, not just downward
- measured in a quiet window: run `tests/motion/smooth.html` first as a control; if the
  control shows any frame over 33 ms, the host is busy and the page's numbers are noise

## What the harness still cannot tell you

Upstream's `verify.md` says it plainly: *"Whether the motion is smooth. Contiguous frames
prove the clip advances; they do not prove it advances evenly."* `motion_probe.py` closes
most of that gap and does not close all of it. Watch the contact sheet for a move that
lurches, reverses, or stalls in the middle, and watch the sparkline the probe writes: a
curve with a flat shoulder is an act that stops dead mid-travel, which no single number
reports.

One known, accepted inconsistency: `scripts/scroll/scrollcraft.css` line 98 still carries
`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { html { scroll-behavior: auto } }`. It only
disables smooth anchor jumping and touches no act, and the engine is never edited, so it
stays — documented here rather than silently tolerated.

## Related

[`scroll/devices.md`](scroll/devices.md) · [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md) ·
[`performance.md`](performance.md) ·
[`motion.md`](motion.md) · `scripts/motion_probe.py` · `scripts/scroll/sc-smooth.js` ·
FEEDBACK.md F-011, F-012, F-013.

1	# TASTE.md — Antons smakprofil, läst ur katalogen
2	
3	Skriven 2026-09-04 av Claude efter egen läsning av alla 89 källor (55 råa skärmbilder Anton
4	sparat själv, 34 Refero-exporter) som bilder och text. Anteckningarna bakom:
5	`taste/notes-raw-read.md`, `taste/notes-refero-read.md`. Profilen beskriver **harmonin**, hur
6	typ, bild, yta och rörelse förhåller sig till varandra, inte vilka färger eller typsnitt som
7	ska användas. Färg och typsnitt härleds fortfarande ur varumärket (Tier 0–2); det här säger
8	hur de ska *samspela* när de väl är valda, och vad som aldrig får hända.
9	
10	Hur den används: `design/SKILL.md` Step 1b läser den när beställaren är Anton eller när
11	briefen saknar referenser. Reference-lockens preserve-lista prövas mot avsnitt 4.
12	Bake-offens riktningar seedas ur avsnitt 3.
13	
14	---
15	
16	## 1. Det genomgående temat: en auktoritet per sida
17	
18	Varje sparad sida låter **en enda sak** bära uppmärksamheten, och allt annat drar sig
19	tillbaka för den. Det är den enskilt tydligaste regeln i materialet, och den håller tvärs alla
20	kategorier:
21	
22	| Auktoriteten | Då gör typen | Då gör bilden | Då gör ytan | Exempel |
23	|---|---|---|---|---|
24	| **Typen** (ordmärke eller rubrik i viewport-bredd) | 100–265 px, en vikt, stram | tyst: liten, bredvid, eller bakom typen som ett lager | flat papper eller flat färgblock | Garden Eight, Shelby Kay, SpringSummer, Busy Bee, Indoek, Studio Ag, Mattis, Magnetism |
25	| **Fotot** (fullbleed, mörkt eller överexponerat) | vikt 300, ljus, stor men luftig, lägger sig i fotots mörka del | allt | ingen: fotot är ytan | Squarespace, Planhat, Apollo, Amrit, Montoni, Geon, Rogo, Diamond Rose |
26	| **Ytan/materialet** (papper, linne, terrakotta, celadon) | medelstor, gärna serif, får ta plats men inte skrika | plates bredvid texten, aldrig under | bär allt: ton-på-ton, hårlinjer, inga skuggor | Raus, Beautiful, Palais, TOMO, alet, Miti, Caractère Bois, Kinhive |
27	| **Produkten** (objektet ofriat i mitten) | uppercase 500 i små grader, eller helt tyst | ett objekt i tomrum | mörk eller flat | ORYZO, Busy Bee, Hungry Tiger, Aarke, David, Altitude |
28	| **Rörelsen** | tyst | tyst eller suddig | ljus, luftig | Perplexity, dope.security, alet, Bumble, Comet |
29	
30	Sidor där två av dessa konkurrerar finns inte i materialet. Det är därför Antons "för
31	snarlika"-kritik träffar de kedjebyggen som la stor serif *och* starkt foto *och* accentfärg
32	i samma fold: tre auktoriteter är ingen.
33	
34	**Regel:** namnge auktoriteten innan koden. Allt som inte är auktoriteten går ner ett steg
35	i vikt, storlek eller mättnad.
36	
37	## 2. Fem relationer som återkommer
38	
39	1. **Tyst typ ↔ stark bild, stark typ ↔ tyst bild.** Weight 300 vid 64–110 px sitter alltid på
40	   ett foto eller ett tomt papper. Fet eller kondenserad display (Busy Bee 238 px, Shelby Kay
41	   265 px) sitter alltid på en flat yta. Undantaget som håller: tung grotesk *genom* ett orört
42	   foto (Indoek, What Matters, Go RVing, Mattis), men bara när typen är tung nog att tåla
43	   fotot. Tunn typ på ett ljust, brusigt foto förekommer noll gånger.
44	2. **Ett papper, en accent.** 69 av 89 har en varm eller kall "paper"-yta och exakt en
45	   kromatisk färg som gör en sak: CTA, understryk, ordmärke. Vit yta är sällsynt (Paper,
46	   Not Real, Andre Candido, Aarke) och då är den *varmvit* och typen är svart. Två accenter
47	   förekommer bara i consumer/playful (OLIPOP, Palais, Shepherd).
48	3. **Struktur med hårlinjer och ton-på-ton, aldrig med kort.** Skuggade kort: 0 av 89 där
49	   Anton valt (de finns i tre AI-mallar, som defaults). Djup kommer av cream-på-cream,
50	   1 px-linjer, överlapp och färgband som byter *material* mellan sektioner.
51	4. **Storlekskontrast 5–15×, inte 2–3×.** Display 64–265 px mot body 14–17 px. En sida med
52	   "h1 48 / h2 32 / p 16" finns inte i materialet. Mellanrubriker är antingen små uppercase
53	   kickers (11–13 px, tracking 0.1–0.2 em) eller lika stora som display. Mellanläget saknas.
54	5. **Rundning är ett beslut.** Antingen 0–3 px (Amrit, Apollo, alet, Not Real, Squarespace,
55	   NGLM) eller stor och avsiktlig (Raus 20/40, Bumble 16–24, pill-knappar 999). Ingen ligger
56	   på 8 px-default.
57	
58	## 3. Per kategori: harmonin, och vad som bär
59	
60	Kategorierna är de i `categories.md`. "Bär" = auktoriteten enligt avsnitt 1.
61	
62	### product-focused (SaaS, verktyg)
63	Bär: **fotot som stämning** (Planhat, Sanity, Rogo, HappyRobot) eller **produkten som bild**
64	(Paper, Solva, customer.io, Operator). Typ: neo-grotesk 300–400 i stor grad, stram tracking,
65	eller en två-tons rubrik (Paper: mörk första rad, grå fortsättning). Ytan: mörk eller varmvit,
66	aldrig lila. Rörelse: subtil, aldrig "breathing". Siffror som textur (Hark, RRE, NGLM) i
67	display-grad med liten etikett, ruled. **Det Anton avvisar här:** feature-grid med ikoner,
68	"trusted by"-logg-rad som fyllning, tre lika kort. I mallarna han sparat (Nura, Solva, Areto)
69	är det heron han sparat, inte resten.
70	
71	### portfolio / studio
72	Bär: **typen som verket.** Ordmärke eller påstående i viewport-bredd (Magnetism, Garden
73	Eight, Studio Ag, Mattis, Example, Orix). Arbetet i asymmetriskt grid, metadata i marginalen
74	(mono eller 11 px uppercase). Ingen CTA-fyllning; kontakt är en textrad. Ytan: papper eller
75	flat färgblock; Mattis och Lucci visar att ett helt orange eller rött band är tillåtet när
76	typen är tung grotesk.
77	
78	### institutional
79	Bär: **lugn skala.** Få enheter, stor luft, en sats i taget (Hark, RRE, Montoni, Equity Fund).
80	Typ: grotesk 300–400 eller en lugn serif, aldrig kondenserad. Data som textur är kategorins
81	signatur. Foto: landskap eller material, mörkat. Rörelse: nästan ingen.
82	
83	### editorial
84	Bär: **ytan + rytmen.** Papper, kolumner, kickers, plates bredvid texten, journal-rytm (Raus,
85	Indoek, Caractère Bois, Dovetail, Redbrick, Aevi). Serif tillåten och vanlig, men alltid med
86	en grotesk eller mono för etiketter, aldrig serif på etiketter.
87	
88	### hospitality / plats
89	Bär: **fotot.** Typen anpassar sig: ljus 300-serif *i* fotots mörka del (Amrit, Apollo,
90	Montoni, Geon) eller display-serif på papper *bredvid* fotot (Raus, Miti, Diamond Rose).
91	Alltid en enda handling (boka/sök) i en enda färg. Ordmärke i viewport-bredd är vanligt
92	(Diamond Rose, Maloot, Miti-kurvan).
93	
94	### consumer-brand
95	Bär: **produkten och färgen.** Flat färgblock, produkten ofriad i mitten, condensed/fet
96	display 100–240 px (Busy Bee, Hungry Tiger, David, Lucci, Deon Libra). Marquee-remsan som
97	avdelare hör hit och ingen annanstans. Färgen får vara lek; typen är sign-painting.
98	
99	### luxury-craft
100	Bär: **ett objekt i tomrum.** Cream-typ, uppercase 500 i små grader, allt annat tyst (ORYZO,
101	Diabla, Dix Hectares, Aarke, Geon). Material före dekor: sten, kork, linne, stål.
102	
103	### playful
104	Bär: **färgen eller rörelsen** (Bumble, OLIPOP, Palais, Andre Candido). Illustration bara som
105	teckning eller 3D-objekt, aldrig som ikon-set. Två accenter tillåtna, inte tre.
106	
107	## 4. Beslutsregler för typsnitt och bild, så att de samspelar
108	
109	Dessa är de regler kedjan ska pröva varje val mot. De gäller *utöver* varumärkets egna
110	tokens.
111	
112	1. **Välj auktoritet först, typsnitt sedan.** Bär fotot: välj ett snitt som tål vikt 300 i
113	   80 px (neo-grotesk eller en serif med låg kontrast). Bär typen: välj ett snitt med
114	   karaktär i 150 px+ (kondenserad grotesk, didone, eller ett ovanligt display-serif) och
115	   håll fotot litet. Bär ytan: en lugn serif i 40–70 px och grotesk för allt annat.
116	2. **Två snitt, aldrig tre, och rollerna korsar aldrig.** Ett för röst (display + body eller
117	   bara display), ett för register (etiketter, siffror, nav). Mono får bara vara register.
118	   Serif får aldrig vara etikett.
119	3. **Bilden väljs efter hur mycket typ den ska bära.** Typ över foto kräver antingen ett
120	   mörkt/överexponerat parti där typen får stå (mät kontrasten under den ljusaste ramen,
121	   Step 5), eller en typvikt ≥ 700. Annars läggs fotot bredvid texten som en plate med
122	   caption. Aldrig scrim över hela bilden som räddning.
123	4. **Ett papper, en accent, och accenten gör en sak.** Bestäm vad (CTA, understryk,
124	   ordmärke, en siffra) och låt den inte göra något annat. Andra accenten kräver kategori
125	   consumer/playful och en motivering i beslutsledgern.
126	5. **Sektioner byter material, inte bara bakgrund.** När sidan behöver en ny akt: helt
127	   färgband, mörk-till-ljus inversion, eller papper-till-foto. Inte "grå sektion".
128	6. **Kontrast i skala, inte i vikt.** Display minst 5× body. Mellanrubriker antingen som
129	   kickers (små, tracking) eller lika stora som display. Aldrig en 32 px-mellannivå.
130	7. **Djup utan skugga.** Hårlinjer, ton-på-ton, överlapp, inversion. Skugga bara på en
131	   flytande komponent (modal, sökfält) och då knappt synlig.
132	8. **Rörelse bara där typ och bild är tysta.** Är auktoriteten typ eller foto: reveal och
133	   pin räcker. Är auktoriteten rörelsen: låt typen vara 300 och bilden suddig.
134	   *Precisering (r6, 2026-09-06):* när briefen uttryckligen ber om scrollkoreografi är
135	   rörelsen auktoriteten **i set-piece-akten**: där viker typ och foto (typ i vikt 300,
