1	# The device kit, condensed
2	
3	Nine ways scroll can drive the page. Pick per beat, never per page: ≥4 device
4	families, never the same one twice running. Every act publishes `--sc-p` (0–1)
5	on itself, so bespoke CSS can ride the same value the kit devices use. Full
6	depth, worked examples, and every trap: `upstream/scroll-craft/.../references/devices.md`.
7	
8	| # | Device | Syntax | Span / rate | One-line rule |
9	|---|---|---|---|---|
10	| 1 | `scrub` | `data-sc-act="scrub" data-sc-span="2.6" data-sc-dwell="0.35"` on the section; `data-sc-scrub data-sc-src="…"` on the `<video>` | span 2.2–3.0 for a hero | ≤2 per page. The wheel scrubs a pre-rendered clip; spend it on the open |
11	| 2 | `pin` | `data-sc-act="pin" data-sc-span="3"` | span ≥1.2 (below that, progress jumps 0→1 in one notch) | The frame holds, copy states cross over inside it |
12	| 3 | `pan` | `data-sc-act="pan" data-sc-span="3.2"`; rail gets `data-sc-pan="0.08"` | ~1vh per item + 1 | Lateral = breadth, not hierarchy. Overflow must be measured, not assumed |
13	| 4 | `reveal` | `data-sc-reveal="up|down|left|right|iris" data-sc-reveal-at="0.15 0.55"` | — | `clip-path` wipe = change of state. `iris` once per page at most |
14	| 5 | `kinetic` | `data-sc-kinetic="lines|words|chars"` on a cued heading | — | Lines almost always right, chars ~never. One kinetic headline per act |
15	| 6 | `parallax` | `data-sc-parallax="-0.6"` | rate is **hundreds of px total travel**, not a fraction — usable range 0.3–1.5 (framed), 1–2 (full-bleed) | Never on body copy. 3 layers is plenty |
16	| 7 | `count` | `data-sc-count="0 4,200" data-sc-count-at="0.1 0.5"` | 1.2–1.8s outside an act (`data-sc-count-ms`) | Only real numbers. No verified figure, no counter |
17	| 8 | `flow` + `in` | `data-sc-in data-sc-stagger="70"` on the wrap | stagger 30–80ms | The rest of the page. Fires once, opacity+14px rise, ~620ms ease-out |
18	| 9 | pointer: `tilt` / `magnet` / `spotlight` | `data-sc-tilt="7"` (5–9°), `data-sc-magnet="0.28"` (0.2–0.35, CTA only), `data-sc-spotlight` (publishes `--sc-mx`/`--sc-my`) | — | Gated to `(hover:hover) and (pointer:fine)`. Never gated on reduced motion (F-011, superseded 2026-09-07) |
19	
20	`drift` (`data-sc-drift="#0A0806"` on an act) is not a device, it's a
21	property: the page ground interpolates toward it while the act is live. 3–5
22	stops, one theme family. On a page of many *short* acts several can be
23	part-way through at once — paint grounds per section instead of drifting; see
24	upstream §10.
25	
26	## The engine: GSAP + Lenis (house default from 2026-09-24)
27	
28	**Every new build animates with GSAP** (+ScrollTrigger, SplitText when text is
29	split) **and Lenis.** Scrollcraft (`scripts/scroll/`) stays only for pages already
30	built on it — do not port an existing scrollcraft page to GSAP+Lenis just because
31	it's the new default. **Never mix the two engines on one page**: two scroll owners
32	is two RAF loops fighting for the same frame. Anton's instruction: GSAP+Lenis for
33	all animations, applied wherever the motion fits the design and elements of each
34	page.
35	
36	Vendored locally from `scripts/motion/vendor/` (gsap 3.15.0, ScrollTrigger,
37	SplitText, lenis 1.3.26 + `lenis.css`) — copy the whole folder into the build's
38	`assets/vendor/`; never a CDN at runtime. GSAP 3.13+ including SplitText is free.
39	
40	The init, verbatim — house deviations from Lenis's own defaults, each explained
41	once here so no builder reads the Lenis README and takes the default instead:
42	
43	```js
44	var lenis = new Lenis({ autoRaf: false, anchors: true, respectReducedMotion: false, lerp: 0.075, wheelMultiplier: 0.6 });
45	window.__lenis = lenis;
46	gsap.ticker.add(function (time) { lenis.raf(time * 1000); });
47	gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(500, 33);
48	lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update);
49	```
50	
51	- **`respectReducedMotion: false`.** Lenis's own default is `true`, which would
52	  silently switch off all motion for Anton, whose Windows runs with animation
53	  effects off (house rule F-011 / CARL design decision 2026-09-07). Rörelse spelar
54	  alltid — motion always plays.
55	- **`anchors: true`.** Lenis's default is `false`, which breaks in-page anchor
56	  links silently — no error, they just stop scrolling to the target.
57	- **`autoRaf: false`, driven by `gsap.ticker`.** `gsap.ticker` is the only RAF
58	  driver on the page; Lenis's own rAF loop would be a second one racing it.
59	- **`gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(500, 33)`, not `0`.** With `0`, one stalled frame (GC, a GPU queue, a
60	  first paint) hands Lenis the whole lost time at once and a running `scrollTo` jumps to catch
61	  up — measured Alunix V3g 2026-09-25: 490–724 px in a single frame after a click. With
62	  `(500, 33)` a stall over 500 ms counts as 33 ms: the scroll pauses and resumes (max step
63	  38–90 px over four runs). Lenis and ScrollTrigger share the same clamped clock, so they
64	  stay in sync.
65	- **`lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update)`**
66	  keep GSAP's tab-blur catch-up off and ScrollTrigger's cached positions synced to
67	  Lenis's virtual scroll on every frame.
68	- **`window.__lenis`** is the dev hook every jump-test drives:
69	  `lenis.scrollTo(el, {immediate:true})`, never `window.scrollTo`.
70	
71	No `scrollerProxy` (Lenis scrolls the real page, not a virtual container). No CSS
72	`scroll-behavior: smooth` anywhere — it fights Lenis's own smoothing.
73	
74	**Iframes.** `lenis.css` sets `pointer-events: none` on iframes while smooth-scroll
75	is active — wanted behaviour for scroll-driven embeds (a showcase iframe the reader
76	scrolls *past*). For an embed the reader should scroll *inside*, set
77	`data-lenis-prevent` on it.
78	
79	### Scrollcraft device → GSAP equivalent
80	
81	| Scrollcraft | GSAP + Lenis |
82	|---|---|
83	| `scrub` (`data-sc-act=scrub`) | ScrollTrigger `scrub: true` timeline |
84	| `pin` | `pin: true`, created **once** at init |
85	| `pan` | pinned timeline, `xPercent` |
86	| `reveal` | `ScrollTrigger.batch` or a per-element trigger, fail toward visible |
87	| `kinetic` | SplitText `type:'lines,words,chars', mask:'lines'` + per-word `white-space: nowrap`; the mask needs `padding-bottom` with an equal negative margin so descenders survive |
88	| `parallax` | `yPercent` scrub |
89	| `count` | tween on a plain object + `snap` / `gsap.utils.snap` |
90	| `tilt` / `magnet` | `gsap.quickTo`, gated `(hover: hover)` |
91	| grid dissolve | `stagger: {grid, from:'random'}` |
92	| `responsive` (`gsap.matchMedia`) | `gsap.matchMedia()` |
93	
94	### Load-bearing rules
95	
96	- Create every ScrollTrigger **in page order.**
97	- **Never mix `scrub` and `toggleActions` on one trigger.**
98	- The **last element on the page** uses `end: 'bottom bottom'`.
99	- **With Lenis, use `scrub: true`, not a numeric scrub.** Lenis is the ONE
100	  smoothing layer on the page — a numeric scrub value stacks a second lag on top
101	  of it. Measured jank in V3f's showcase, 2026-09-24.
102	- **A pin is created once at init and is never killed/recreated on user
103	  interaction.** V3f's click handler did that and produced a hard, visible
104	  transition where the pin snapped instead of holding.
105	- **`end` is set in pixels via a function, with `invalidateOnRefresh: true` —
106	  never a `'+=Nvh'` string.** ScrollTrigger silently ignores the `vh` suffix on
107	  that shorthand — measured V3f R5.
108	
109	- **An iframe inside a pinned element needs an explicit `pinSpacer`.** ScrollTrigger re-parents
110	  the pinned element into its own pin-spacer on every `refresh()`, and a re-parented iframe
111	  reloads its document. If that iframe's `load` then asks for a refresh, the page runs a
112	  reload loop for the whole visit (measured Alunix V3f/V3g 2026-09-25: 6–12 reloads per
113	  iframe per pass, ~1/s, and the thesis headline two sections away lost half its frames).
114	  Put a wrapper in the markup (`<div class="x-pin-spacer"><div class="x-stage">…`) and pass
115	  `pinSpacer: '.x-pin-spacer'`. Never call `refresh()` from an iframe's `load`; an iframe
116	  has fixed dimensions and cannot change the outer layout.
117	- **Every scrubbed trigger uses `scrub: true`** — hero and thesis pins included, not only
118	  the one being edited this round. A numeric scrub anywhere is a second smoothing layer.
119	- **House pace (Anton 2026-09-25: "scrollen går för snabbt … man kastas förbi kortet").**
120	  Lenis `wheelMultiplier: 0.6` and `lerp: 0.075` — one wheel notch moves ~60 px and glides.
121	  A pin whose content the reader must watch happen (a card flip, a step change) spans at
122	  least 200 vh of scroll; nothing the reader should see may complete within one or two
123	  notches. Slower is only better if it stays even: verify with `section_probe.py`.
124	- **A timeline driven by `.progress(p)` must last exactly 1.** Tweens placed at absolute
125	  positions on a 0–1 scale end before 1, so the timeline is shorter and `progress(p)` runs
126	  it out of step with everything else driven by `p` — measured V3g 2026-09-25: late steps
127	  never faded in, and scrolling back left the active text at opacity 0. End every such
128	  timeline with `tl.set({}, {}, 1)`, and check a step by jumping to it AND by scrolling back
129	  to it, not only on the first forward pass.
130	- **Check: `scripts/section_probe.py URL --baseline <previous.json>`** after every round,
131	  on the WHOLE page, not only the edited section. It fails on an iframe that loads more
132	  than once, on any refresh during the scroll pass, and on any section whose p95 frame time
133	  got worse than the approved baseline. Verified to fail on V3f and V3g before the fix.
134	
135	### Skills to load before the first line of motion code
136	
137	In order: `lenis` → `gsap-core` → `gsap-scrolltrigger` → `gsap-timeline` →
138	`gsap-plugins` (if SplitText/Flip) → `gsap-performance` → `gsap-utils` (if
139	needed). Plus the UI-skills registry's `ibelick/fixing-motion-performance` — see
140	[`skill-orchestration.md`](../skill-orchestration.md).
141	
142	## The cue contract — what verification actually catches you on
143	
144	`data-sc-cue="from [to [rampIn [rampOut]]]"`, all in act progress 0–1.
145	
146	| Form | Behaviour |
147	|---|---|
148	| `"0.2"` | fades in at 0.2, **holds to the end of the act** |
149	| `"0.1 0.6"` | in, plateau, out (ramps default 30% of window each) |
150	| `"0 0.78 0"` | **greet**: full opacity at act start, then fades — the hero form |
151	| `"0 1 0 0"` | **greet and hold**: full at p=0, no ramp either end |
152	
153	**The plateau is the point.** Without one, a cue is a triangle that touches full
154	opacity for a single instant, so the reader has to stop on exactly the right
155	pixel to see the line at full strength and every heading reads slightly faded.
156	`"0.1 0.9 0.15 0.4"` — fast in, long slow out — is the confident form. Cue
157	windows on a pinned act **overlap by design**, roughly 15% of the act: the
158	outgoing line is still fading while the next arrives, and a gap between cues
159	reads as a loading failure.
160	
161	Five rules, each one a real bug this fixture has caught:
162	
163	- **A hero cue needs the greet form.** A plain `"0 0.7"` means the first
164	  screen every visitor sees has no headline on it.
165	- **The last act's cue must hold** (one value). A two-value close cue fades
166	  the CTA out before the page ends.
167	- **Only the last act may hold.** A one-value cue on a *middle* pinned act
168	  stays lit through the whole un-pin slide — the line travels a full viewport
169	  up, crosses fixed chrome, overlaps the next section. Invisible until
170	  measured; shows up as a contrast failure nobody meant.
171	- **Ground or greet.** A pinned stage is fully visible ~1vh *before* its own
172	  progress leaves 0. A plain two-value first cue shows an empty stage for
173	  that whole travel — give the act a ground (image/colour already doing
174	  work) or open with a greet cue.
175	- **Clip time ≠ cue time.** A `scrub` clip is mapped across the stage's
176	  *entire visible life* (default), not across the pinned travel, because the
177	  stage is on screen for a viewport before the pin starts and after it ends.
178	  Cues keep using `p` (they belong to the pin); the clip uses a separately
179	  computed `vp`. Reaching for `data-sc-clip-map="travel"` reintroduces the
180	  freeze — there's almost no reason to.
181	
182	Two more that a harness will not catch by itself:
183	
184	- **Pan overflow must be measured, not assumed.** The rail travels exactly
185	  `scrollWidth - viewport`; a rail narrower than the viewport travels **zero**
186	  and the act reads as a still. `rail.scrollWidth - innerWidth` — check it,
187	  don't guess.
188	- **Parallax rate is hundreds of pixels total, not a viewport fraction** — see
189	  the table above. A rate of 0.35 across three viewport-heights of scroll is
190	  35px: invisible.
191	
192	Composing an act: devices stack (a pinned stage can hold a scrub clip, a
193	parallax layer, a kinetic headline, a spotlight at once), but one thing is the
194	reason the act exists — say that thing in one sentence or the act has none.
195	
196	## The playhead is lerped (§1)
197	
198	The mechanism the whole kit's smoothness rests on, and the one F-012 kept
199	being blamed on. **Scroll never writes `currentTime`.** It writes a *target*,
200	and a standalone rAF loop walks the clip toward that target at a fixed
201	fraction per frame:
202	
203	> *"Wheel events do not arrive at a constant rate, so a 1:1 write reproduces
204	> every gap in them and the clip reads as a stutter rather than a glide."*
205	
206	Three mechanisms, all on by default:
207	
208	- **Lerp 0.18 per frame.** `data-sc-lerp` overrides it, on the mount root for
209	  the whole page or on a single `<video>`. **Clamped to 0.02–1 and never read
210	  as 0** — a 0 lerp is a playhead that never moves. Reach for an override only
211	  when a page's clips are short enough that 0.18 visibly lags the hand.
212	  Worldflight wants 0.12 instead; see [`pace.md`](pace.md).
213	- **Deadband: 8 ms desktop, 20 ms mobile.** A write smaller than that costs a
214	  seek and shows nothing; on a phone it costs more than it shows.
215	- **Seek coalescing.** No seek is queued while the decoder is still resolving
216	  the last one. *"A fast flick otherwise piles seeks up and freezes the clip."*
217	
218	An offscreen clip that has already reached its target stops being touched at
219	all. (Upstream states the offscreen skip without a threshold value; the 0.002
220	figure belongs to `shoot.mjs`'s settle test, below, not to this skip.)
221	
222	This applies to **every** scrub clip on the page, act or worldflight. It is
223	also why the shooter waits for the playhead to arrive before each frame:
224	
225	> *"A frame captured mid-lerp is a frame the page never actually holds."*
226	
227	`shoot.mjs` settles on `|current − target| < 0.002 && !seeking`. Any harness
228	the chain runs against a scrubbed page inherits that requirement — a
229	screenshot taken mid-lerp makes the run unrepeatable, not merely imprecise.
230	
231	Upstream also drops the damping to 1.0 (no smoothing at all) under reduced
232	motion. **That branch does not port: F-011.** The lerp is unconditional here,
233	which is the correct behaviour anyway — it is a smoothing mechanism, not an
234	effect, and turning it off is what produces the stepping fault.
235	
236	## Layered scenes: where the premium feel comes from (§6)
237	
238	Ported from `devices.md` § 6, measured off a reference premium site and proven
239	on a live build. A flat page moves as one sheet; a layered page is a stack of
240	cut-out planes sliding past each other, and *"the eye reads that differential
241	motion as depth before it reads anything else."* It is the single biggest
242	difference between a page that feels built and one that feels assembled, and
243	it costs three transparent images and a multiplier each.
244	
245	- **Plan the planes back to front.** Far ridge, mid ridge, the product, then a
246	  **foreground plane in front of the product**. The product sits between mid
247	  and front, so the foreground overtakes it as the reader scrolls. That
248	  overtaking is the move.
249	- **Small rate differences, not big ones.** The reference hero lags the far
250	  plane **31%** behind the page, the mid plane **17%**, the product **20%**,
251	  and foreground and copy travel at exactly **1×**. Adjacent planes differ by
252	  **10–30%**. Larger stops reading as distance and starts reading as things
253	  sliding around. **Copy always rides at 1×.**
254	- **Shape the foreground for the product.** A straight-edged foreground covers
255	  the product's CTA within a few hundred pixels of scroll. Cut it so it dips
256	  where the product is and rises at the edges, and the button stays in view
257	  two to three times as long.
258	- **Every plane is solid below its silhouette.** Cut-out art that fades to
259	  transparent at the bottom lets the plane behind show through as the planes
260	  separate. Fill each column solid from its first opaque pixel down.
261	- **Fade the section floor.** Planes travel past the section's bottom edge and
262	  are clipped there. A gradient to the page ground over the last 200–300 px,
263	  layered above every plane, hides the clip line at any scroll position.
264	
265	Three traps, each of which cost a round of fixes:
266	
267	- A global `img { max-width: 100% }` shrinks an absolutely positioned plane to
268	  the viewport on phones, so the far layer never shows. **Planes carry
269	  `max-width: none` and a fixed pixel width.**
270	- **Never `transition: transform` on a parallaxed element.** A reveal class is
271	  the usual culprit. The transition eases every per-frame scroll write over
272	  its own duration, and on a phone that reads as the product lagging a full
273	  second behind the thumb. Parallaxed elements transition **opacity only**.
274	- Replacing a plane's art under the same filename ships nothing to a phone
275	  holding the old bytes. **New art gets a new name.**
276	
277	`data-sc-parallax` and a raw scroll multiplier are the same tool in different
278	units. What matters is the **ratio between planes**, not the absolute travel.
279	
280	## The premium fade-in, exactly (§8)
281	
282	The `flow` + `in` device is most of the page, so its defaults decide how the
283	page feels between the acts:
284	
285	| Ingredient | Value |
286	|---|---|
287	| Opacity | 0 → 1 |
288	| Rise | **~14 px** |
289	| Duration | **~620 ms**, ease-out |
290	| Stagger | **30–80 ms**, children in reading order |
291	| Trigger | IntersectionObserver, `-12%` bottom root margin, **fires once** |
292	
293	- **A fade with no rise reads as a loading glitch.** A rise **past 24 px reads
294	  as a slide.** 14 px is the band, not a starting point to tune upward.
295	- The `-12%` margin fires the reveal when the reader is looking, not when the
296	  first pixel clears the fold.
297	- `data-sc-in` is what the engine watches. Without it nothing fires and the
298	  stagger children stay hidden.
299	- **Content that re-hides on the way back up is a defect, not an effect.**
300	- *"Larger, slower, or bouncier is never more premium; the restraint is the
301	  signal."*
302	
303	**A flow section directly after a pinned act takes reduced padding.** The
304	pinned stage needs a full viewport to scroll off, and full `--sc-section`
305	padding on top of that delays the flow section's first content by another
306	screen. The harness will not call it dead scroll — correctly, the stage is
307	moving — and the reader still sees a near-empty screen. Cut the block padding
308	there and start the first reveal near `p = 0`.
309	
310	## Rail settle on `pan` (§3)
311	
312	Lateral travel alone reads as a slideshow on rails. **Give the rail's items a
313	staggered settle driven from `--sc-p`** and they read as a drawer being
314	pulled instead.
315	
316	- **Exempt the first item** — a `pan` act needs its opening content already
317	  present.
318	- **Floor the opacity around 0.55**, so a not-yet-settled card reads as
319	  arriving rather than as failing to load.
320	
321	Upstream gates the settle to `prefers-reduced-motion` — **utgår, F-011**.
322	The settle always runs. What *does* survive from
323	the same passage is the reachability requirement, which is not a motion
324	preference at all: a `pan` rail's transform **is** the navigation, so nothing
325	may zero it and park the act on its first screenful. Every item in a rail
326	stays reachable, and that is checked on the sheet, not assumed.
327	
328	Two more, from the same section:
329	
330	- **Card copy is read while cropped.** Items enter and leave through the
331	  viewport edges, so a heading is half-shown for most of its life, and two
332	  half-headings side by side can read as a third word (`TRACE` beside
333	  `EVALUATE` becoming `RE EVALUATE`). Keep card headings to one or two short
334	  words and expect every line to be read partially cut off.
335	- If three items do not reach half a viewport of overflow, **the fix is more
336	  rail, not wider cards**: put the act's heading in as the first item and a
337	  closing note as the last. Both earn their place, and they add the width the
338	  travel needs.
339	
340	## Devices that cannot share an element (§9)
341	
342	**`magnet`, `parallax` and `cue` all write `transform`.** The magnet writes
343	every frame in its own rAF loop, so it silently wins and the cue's entrance
344	rise is discarded — a visible animation lost to a race, with nothing in the
345	console.
346	
347	- On a magnetic CTA, set **`data-sc-rise="0"`** so the cue writes a no-op
348	  instead of losing to the magnet.
349	- A cued element that wants its own continuous transform drives an **inner
350	  wrapper** from `--sc-p` in CSS, rather than stacking a second device on the
351	  same node.
352	
353	All three pointer devices **interpolate toward** the pointer rather than
354	tracking it directly: *"direct tracking reads as artificial because it carries
355	no momentum."* They stay gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` so
356	touch never fires a false hover — that gate is a pointer-capability query, not
357	a motion preference, and it stands.
358	The reduced-motion half of the same sentence does not port (F-011).
359	
360	## Kinetic type: the mask and the re-split (§5)
361	
362	Each unit slides up from **behind a mask**, so it enters from a clean edge
363	rather than simply fading.
364	
365	- **Line masks must reserve room for descenders.** A mask clipped to the line
366	  box shears the tails off g, y, p and j, *"and that is the single most common
367	  way this effect looks broken."*
368	- **Line splitting measures real line boxes, so it re-runs after
369	  `document.fonts.ready`.** Do not call it on text still loading its face. The
370	  same `fonts.ready` handle earns its place twice over: a webfont swapping in
371	  changes the measured height of every copy block, so anything sized against
372	  those blocks (a scrim plate, a rail) is wrong until it re-measures.
373	- Lines are almost always right; words for a short punch line; characters
374	  approximately never, *"because it turns reading into waiting."*
375	- **One kinetic headline per act, at most.**
376	
377	## What makes a `count` land (§7)
378	
379	- **Ease out, hard.** A cubic ease-out, so most of the distance goes by in the
380	  first third and the last digits settle slowly. *"A linear count reads as a
381	  slot machine."*
382	- **1.2–1.8 s.** Under a second and the reader misses that it moved; past two
383	  and they are waiting for a number they have already guessed.
384	- **Fires at half visibility, once**, so the reader is looking at it when it
385	  starts, and it never re-runs on the way back up.
386	- **Pair it with the fade.** A counter inside a `data-sc-in` stack rises in
387	  with its label and starts ticking as it arrives — *"the same numbers static
388	  on the page read as a spreadsheet."*
389	- Write the target exactly as it should render, commas included; the engine
390	  strips them before parsing and applies `tabular-nums` so the layout does not
391	  jitter.
392	
393	**A concept, fictional or pre-launch brand has no verified figures, so it has
394	no counters.** The device suits a SaaS or agency page and will look good in
395	the score table, *"which is exactly the trap: every number you could put in it
396	would be invented."* Decide this before designing an act around a number, not
397	after. Real brand, real stats, or a different device.
398	
399	## Appendix: pattern vocabulary
400	
401	Named patterns from taste-skill § 10, carried here so orchestrator, builder
402	and reviewer name the same thing. It is a **vocabulary, not a menu** — several
403	entries below are banned as directions elsewhere in the chain (glassmorphism,
404	holographic foil, carousels, gooey menus) and appear here only so a critique
405	can say which trope it is refusing.
406	
407	- **Hero** — Asymmetric Split · Editorial Manifesto · Video/Media Mask ·
408	  Kinetic-Type · Curtain-Reveal · Scroll-Pinned.
409	- **Nav** — Dock Magnification · Magnetic Button (`data-sc-magnet`) · Gooey
410	  Menu · Dynamic Island · Contextual Radial · Floating Speed Dial · Mega Menu
411	  Reveal.
412	- **Layout** — Bento Grid · Masonry · Chroma Grid · Split-Screen Scroll ·
413	  Sticky-Stack Sections.
414	- **Cards** — Parallax Tilt Card (`data-sc-tilt`) · Spotlight Border Card
415	  (`data-sc-spotlight`) · Glassmorphism Panel · Holographic Foil ·
416	  Tinder Swipe Stack · Morphing Modal.
417	- **Scroll** — Sticky Scroll Stack · Horizontal Scroll Hijack (= `pan`) ·
418	  Locomotive / Sequence Scroll (= `scrub`) · Zoom Parallax · Scroll Progress
419	  Path · Liquid Swipe Transition.
420	- **Galleries** — Dome Gallery · Coverflow Carousel · Drag-to-Pan Grid ·
421	  Accordion Image Slider · Hover Image Trail · Glitch Effect Image.
422	- **Type** — Kinetic Marquee · **Text Mask Reveal** (massive type as a
423	  transparent window onto video — this is K2's letter-window) · Text Scramble
424	  · Circular Text Path · Gradient Stroke Animation · Kinetic Typography Grid.
425	- **Micro** — Particle Explosion Button · Liquid Pull-to-Refresh · Skeleton
426	  Shimmer · Directional Hover-Aware Button · Ripple Click · Animated SVG Line
427	  Drawing · Mesh Gradient Background · Lens Blur Depth.
428	
429	Names alone are not permission. A pattern still has to clear the fingerprint
430	gate, the register, and `../motion.md` before it ships.
431	
432	## Never restyle the engine's classes (AB06, 2026-09-03)
433	
434	Theme the engine only through its six colour tokens and two fonts. A project rule on
435	`.sc-stage`, `.sc-copy`, `.sc-scrim` or any other `.sc-*` class silently wins over the
436	engine: the console then says `[scrollcraft] act "…" will not pin: its stage computes
437	position:relative` and every pinned act scrolls away, leaving its spacer as dead scroll.
438	Read the console for `[scrollcraft]` warnings before anything else in Step 5, and run
439	`scripts/scroll_verify.py` — a blind one-shot cannot see either. The engine is opt-in per
440	grammar (scrub, pin, pan); a page that keeps the chain's own single set-piece + shared
441	reveal does not need it.
442

# The device kit, condensed

Nine ways scroll can drive the page. Pick per beat, never per page: ≥4 device
families, never the same one twice running. Every act publishes `--sc-p` (0–1)
on itself, so bespoke CSS can ride the same value the kit devices use. Full
depth, worked examples, and every trap: `upstream/scroll-craft/.../references/devices.md`.

| # | Device | Syntax | Span / rate | One-line rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `scrub` | `data-sc-act="scrub" data-sc-span="2.6" data-sc-dwell="0.35"` on the section; `data-sc-scrub data-sc-src="…"` on the `<video>` | span 2.2–3.0 for a hero | ≤2 per page. The wheel scrubs a pre-rendered clip; spend it on the open |
| 2 | `pin` | `data-sc-act="pin" data-sc-span="3"` | span ≥1.2 (below that, progress jumps 0→1 in one notch) | The frame holds, copy states cross over inside it |
| 3 | `pan` | `data-sc-act="pan" data-sc-span="3.2"`; rail gets `data-sc-pan="0.08"` | ~1vh per item + 1 | Lateral = breadth, not hierarchy. Overflow must be measured, not assumed |
| 4 | `reveal` | `data-sc-reveal="up|down|left|right|iris" data-sc-reveal-at="0.15 0.55"` | — | `clip-path` wipe = change of state. `iris` once per page at most |
| 5 | `kinetic` | `data-sc-kinetic="lines|words|chars"` on a cued heading | — | Lines almost always right, chars ~never. One kinetic headline per act |
| 6 | `parallax` | `data-sc-parallax="-0.6"` | rate is **hundreds of px total travel**, not a fraction — usable range 0.3–1.5 (framed), 1–2 (full-bleed) | Never on body copy. 3 layers is plenty |
| 7 | `count` | `data-sc-count="0 4,200" data-sc-count-at="0.1 0.5"` | 1.2–1.8s outside an act (`data-sc-count-ms`) | Only real numbers. No verified figure, no counter |
| 8 | `flow` + `in` | `data-sc-in data-sc-stagger="70"` on the wrap | stagger 30–80ms | The rest of the page. Fires once, opacity+14px rise, ~620ms ease-out |
| 9 | pointer: `tilt` / `magnet` / `spotlight` | `data-sc-tilt="7"` (5–9°), `data-sc-magnet="0.28"` (0.2–0.35, CTA only), `data-sc-spotlight` (publishes `--sc-mx`/`--sc-my`) | — | Gated to `(hover:hover) and (pointer:fine)`. Never gated on reduced motion (F-011, superseded 2026-09-07) |

`drift` (`data-sc-drift="#0A0806"` on an act) is not a device, it's a
property: the page ground interpolates toward it while the act is live. 3–5
stops, one theme family. On a page of many *short* acts several can be
part-way through at once — paint grounds per section instead of drifting; see
upstream §10.

## The engine: GSAP + Lenis (house default from 2026-09-24)

**Every new build animates with GSAP** (+ScrollTrigger, SplitText when text is
split) **and Lenis.** Scrollcraft (`scripts/scroll/`) stays only for pages already
built on it — do not port an existing scrollcraft page to GSAP+Lenis just because
it's the new default. **Never mix the two engines on one page**: two scroll owners
is two RAF loops fighting for the same frame. Anton's instruction: GSAP+Lenis for
all animations, applied wherever the motion fits the design and elements of each
page.

Vendored locally from `scripts/motion/vendor/` (gsap 3.15.0, ScrollTrigger,
SplitText, lenis 1.3.26 + `lenis.css`) — copy the whole folder into the build's
`assets/vendor/`; never a CDN at runtime. GSAP 3.13+ including SplitText is free.

The init, verbatim — house deviations from Lenis's own defaults, each explained
once here so no builder reads the Lenis README and takes the default instead:

```js
var lenis = new Lenis({ autoRaf: false, anchors: true, respectReducedMotion: false, lerp: 0.075, wheelMultiplier: 0.6 });
window.__lenis = lenis;
gsap.ticker.add(function (time) { lenis.raf(time * 1000); });
gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(500, 33);
lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update);
```

- **`respectReducedMotion: false`.** Lenis's own default is `true`, which would
  silently switch off all motion for Anton, whose Windows runs with animation
  effects off (house rule F-011 / CARL design decision 2026-09-07). Rörelse spelar
  alltid — motion always plays.
- **`anchors: true`.** Lenis's default is `false`, which breaks in-page anchor
  links silently — no error, they just stop scrolling to the target.
- **`autoRaf: false`, driven by `gsap.ticker`.** `gsap.ticker` is the only RAF
  driver on the page; Lenis's own rAF loop would be a second one racing it.
- **`gsap.ticker.lagSmoothing(500, 33)`, not `0`.** With `0`, one stalled frame (GC, a GPU queue, a
  first paint) hands Lenis the whole lost time at once and a running `scrollTo` jumps to catch
  up — measured Alunix V3g 2026-09-25: 490–724 px in a single frame after a click. With
  `(500, 33)` a stall over 500 ms counts as 33 ms: the scroll pauses and resumes (max step
  38–90 px over four runs). Lenis and ScrollTrigger share the same clamped clock, so they
  stay in sync.
- **`lenis.on('scroll', ScrollTrigger.update)`**
  keep GSAP's tab-blur catch-up off and ScrollTrigger's cached positions synced to
  Lenis's virtual scroll on every frame.
- **`window.__lenis`** is the dev hook every jump-test drives:
  `lenis.scrollTo(el, {immediate:true})`, never `window.scrollTo`.

No `scrollerProxy` (Lenis scrolls the real page, not a virtual container). No CSS
`scroll-behavior: smooth` anywhere — it fights Lenis's own smoothing.

**Iframes.** `lenis.css` sets `pointer-events: none` on iframes while smooth-scroll
is active — wanted behaviour for scroll-driven embeds (a showcase iframe the reader
scrolls *past*). For an embed the reader should scroll *inside*, set
`data-lenis-prevent` on it.

### Scrollcraft device → GSAP equivalent

| Scrollcraft | GSAP + Lenis |
|---|---|
| `scrub` (`data-sc-act=scrub`) | ScrollTrigger `scrub: true` timeline |
| `pin` | `pin: true`, created **once** at init |
| `pan` | pinned timeline, `xPercent` |
| `reveal` | `ScrollTrigger.batch` or a per-element trigger, fail toward visible |
| `kinetic` | SplitText `type:'lines,words,chars', mask:'lines'` + per-word `white-space: nowrap`; the mask needs `padding-bottom` with an equal negative margin so descenders survive |
| `parallax` | `yPercent` scrub |
| `count` | tween on a plain object + `snap` / `gsap.utils.snap` |
| `tilt` / `magnet` | `gsap.quickTo`, gated `(hover: hover)` |
| grid dissolve | `stagger: {grid, from:'random'}` |
| `responsive` (`gsap.matchMedia`) | `gsap.matchMedia()` |

### Load-bearing rules

- Create every ScrollTrigger **in page order.**
- **Never mix `scrub` and `toggleActions` on one trigger.**
- The **last element on the page** uses `end: 'bottom bottom'`.
- **With Lenis, use `scrub: true`, not a numeric scrub.** Lenis is the ONE
  smoothing layer on the page — a numeric scrub value stacks a second lag on top
  of it. Measured jank in V3f's showcase, 2026-09-24.
- **A pin is created once at init and is never killed/recreated on user
  interaction.** V3f's click handler did that and produced a hard, visible
  transition where the pin snapped instead of holding.
- **`end` is set in pixels via a function, with `invalidateOnRefresh: true` —
  never a `'+=Nvh'` string.** ScrollTrigger silently ignores the `vh` suffix on
  that shorthand — measured V3f R5.

- **An iframe inside a pinned element needs an explicit `pinSpacer`.** ScrollTrigger re-parents
  the pinned element into its own pin-spacer on every `refresh()`, and a re-parented iframe
  reloads its document. If that iframe's `load` then asks for a refresh, the page runs a
  reload loop for the whole visit (measured Alunix V3f/V3g 2026-09-25: 6–12 reloads per
  iframe per pass, ~1/s, and the thesis headline two sections away lost half its frames).
  Put a wrapper in the markup (`<div class="x-pin-spacer"><div class="x-stage">…`) and pass
  `pinSpacer: '.x-pin-spacer'`. Never call `refresh()` from an iframe's `load`; an iframe
  has fixed dimensions and cannot change the outer layout.
- **Every scrubbed trigger uses `scrub: true`** — hero and thesis pins included, not only
  the one being edited this round. A numeric scrub anywhere is a second smoothing layer.
- **House pace (Anton 2026-09-25: "scrollen går för snabbt … man kastas förbi kortet").**
  Lenis `wheelMultiplier: 0.6` and `lerp: 0.075` — one wheel notch moves ~60 px and glides.
  A pin whose content the reader must watch happen (a card flip, a step change) spans at
  least 200 vh of scroll; nothing the reader should see may complete within one or two
  notches. Slower is only better if it stays even: verify with `section_probe.py`.
- **A timeline driven by `.progress(p)` must last exactly 1.** Tweens placed at absolute
  positions on a 0–1 scale end before 1, so the timeline is shorter and `progress(p)` runs
  it out of step with everything else driven by `p` — measured V3g 2026-09-25: late steps
  never faded in, and scrolling back left the active text at opacity 0. End every such
  timeline with `tl.set({}, {}, 1)`, and check a step by jumping to it AND by scrolling back
  to it, not only on the first forward pass.
- **Check: `scripts/section_probe.py URL --baseline <previous.json>`** after every round,
  on the WHOLE page, not only the edited section. It fails on an iframe that loads more
  than once, on any refresh during the scroll pass, and on any section whose p95 frame time
  got worse than the approved baseline. Verified to fail on V3f and V3g before the fix.

### Skills to load before the first line of motion code

In order: `lenis` → `gsap-core` → `gsap-scrolltrigger` → `gsap-timeline` →
`gsap-plugins` (if SplitText/Flip) → `gsap-performance` → `gsap-utils` (if
needed). Plus the UI-skills registry's `ibelick/fixing-motion-performance` — see
[`skill-orchestration.md`](../skill-orchestration.md).

## The cue contract — what verification actually catches you on

`data-sc-cue="from [to [rampIn [rampOut]]]"`, all in act progress 0–1.

| Form | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `"0.2"` | fades in at 0.2, **holds to the end of the act** |
| `"0.1 0.6"` | in, plateau, out (ramps default 30% of window each) |
| `"0 0.78 0"` | **greet**: full opacity at act start, then fades — the hero form |
| `"0 1 0 0"` | **greet and hold**: full at p=0, no ramp either end |

**The plateau is the point.** Without one, a cue is a triangle that touches full
opacity for a single instant, so the reader has to stop on exactly the right
pixel to see the line at full strength and every heading reads slightly faded.
`"0.1 0.9 0.15 0.4"` — fast in, long slow out — is the confident form. Cue
windows on a pinned act **overlap by design**, roughly 15% of the act: the
outgoing line is still fading while the next arrives, and a gap between cues
reads as a loading failure.

Five rules, each one a real bug this fixture has caught:

- **A hero cue needs the greet form.** A plain `"0 0.7"` means the first
  screen every visitor sees has no headline on it.
- **The last act's cue must hold** (one value). A two-value close cue fades
  the CTA out before the page ends.
- **Only the last act may hold.** A one-value cue on a *middle* pinned act
  stays lit through the whole un-pin slide — the line travels a full viewport
  up, crosses fixed chrome, overlaps the next section. Invisible until
  measured; shows up as a contrast failure nobody meant.
- **Ground or greet.** A pinned stage is fully visible ~1vh *before* its own
  progress leaves 0. A plain two-value first cue shows an empty stage for
  that whole travel — give the act a ground (image/colour already doing
  work) or open with a greet cue.
- **Clip time ≠ cue time.** A `scrub` clip is mapped across the stage's
  *entire visible life* (default), not across the pinned travel, because the
  stage is on screen for a viewport before the pin starts and after it ends.
  Cues keep using `p` (they belong to the pin); the clip uses a separately
  computed `vp`. Reaching for `data-sc-clip-map="travel"` reintroduces the
  freeze — there's almost no reason to.

Two more that a harness will not catch by itself:

- **Pan overflow must be measured, not assumed.** The rail travels exactly
  `scrollWidth - viewport`; a rail narrower than the viewport travels **zero**
  and the act reads as a still. `rail.scrollWidth - innerWidth` — check it,
  don't guess.
- **Parallax rate is hundreds of pixels total, not a viewport fraction** — see
  the table above. A rate of 0.35 across three viewport-heights of scroll is
  35px: invisible.

Composing an act: devices stack (a pinned stage can hold a scrub clip, a
parallax layer, a kinetic headline, a spotlight at once), but one thing is the
reason the act exists — say that thing in one sentence or the act has none.

## The playhead is lerped (§1)

The mechanism the whole kit's smoothness rests on, and the one F-012 kept
being blamed on. **Scroll never writes `currentTime`.** It writes a *target*,
and a standalone rAF loop walks the clip toward that target at a fixed
fraction per frame:

> *"Wheel events do not arrive at a constant rate, so a 1:1 write reproduces
> every gap in them and the clip reads as a stutter rather than a glide."*

Three mechanisms, all on by default:

- **Lerp 0.18 per frame.** `data-sc-lerp` overrides it, on the mount root for
  the whole page or on a single `<video>`. **Clamped to 0.02–1 and never read
  as 0** — a 0 lerp is a playhead that never moves. Reach for an override only
  when a page's clips are short enough that 0.18 visibly lags the hand.
  Worldflight wants 0.12 instead; see [`pace.md`](pace.md).
- **Deadband: 8 ms desktop, 20 ms mobile.** A write smaller than that costs a
  seek and shows nothing; on a phone it costs more than it shows.
- **Seek coalescing.** No seek is queued while the decoder is still resolving
  the last one. *"A fast flick otherwise piles seeks up and freezes the clip."*

An offscreen clip that has already reached its target stops being touched at
all. (Upstream states the offscreen skip without a threshold value; the 0.002
figure belongs to `shoot.mjs`'s settle test, below, not to this skip.)

This applies to **every** scrub clip on the page, act or worldflight. It is
also why the shooter waits for the playhead to arrive before each frame:

> *"A frame captured mid-lerp is a frame the page never actually holds."*

`shoot.mjs` settles on `|current − target| < 0.002 && !seeking`. Any harness
the chain runs against a scrubbed page inherits that requirement — a
screenshot taken mid-lerp makes the run unrepeatable, not merely imprecise.

Upstream also drops the damping to 1.0 (no smoothing at all) under reduced
motion. **That branch does not port: F-011.** The lerp is unconditional here,
which is the correct behaviour anyway — it is a smoothing mechanism, not an
effect, and turning it off is what produces the stepping fault.

## Layered scenes: where the premium feel comes from (§6)

Ported from `devices.md` § 6, measured off a reference premium site and proven
on a live build. A flat page moves as one sheet; a layered page is a stack of
cut-out planes sliding past each other, and *"the eye reads that differential
motion as depth before it reads anything else."* It is the single biggest
difference between a page that feels built and one that feels assembled, and
it costs three transparent images and a multiplier each.

- **Plan the planes back to front.** Far ridge, mid ridge, the product, then a
  **foreground plane in front of the product**. The product sits between mid
  and front, so the foreground overtakes it as the reader scrolls. That
  overtaking is the move.
- **Small rate differences, not big ones.** The reference hero lags the far
  plane **31%** behind the page, the mid plane **17%**, the product **20%**,
  and foreground and copy travel at exactly **1×**. Adjacent planes differ by
  **10–30%**. Larger stops reading as distance and starts reading as things
  sliding around. **Copy always rides at 1×.**
- **Shape the foreground for the product.** A straight-edged foreground covers
  the product's CTA within a few hundred pixels of scroll. Cut it so it dips
  where the product is and rises at the edges, and the button stays in view
  two to three times as long.
- **Every plane is solid below its silhouette.** Cut-out art that fades to
  transparent at the bottom lets the plane behind show through as the planes
  separate. Fill each column solid from its first opaque pixel down.
- **Fade the section floor.** Planes travel past the section's bottom edge and
  are clipped there. A gradient to the page ground over the last 200–300 px,
  layered above every plane, hides the clip line at any scroll position.

Three traps, each of which cost a round of fixes:

- A global `img { max-width: 100% }` shrinks an absolutely positioned plane to
  the viewport on phones, so the far layer never shows. **Planes carry
  `max-width: none` and a fixed pixel width.**
- **Never `transition: transform` on a parallaxed element.** A reveal class is
  the usual culprit. The transition eases every per-frame scroll write over
  its own duration, and on a phone that reads as the product lagging a full
  second behind the thumb. Parallaxed elements transition **opacity only**.
- Replacing a plane's art under the same filename ships nothing to a phone
  holding the old bytes. **New art gets a new name.**

`data-sc-parallax` and a raw scroll multiplier are the same tool in different
units. What matters is the **ratio between planes**, not the absolute travel.

## The premium fade-in, exactly (§8)

The `flow` + `in` device is most of the page, so its defaults decide how the
page feels between the acts:

| Ingredient | Value |
|---|---|
| Opacity | 0 → 1 |
| Rise | **~14 px** |
| Duration | **~620 ms**, ease-out |
| Stagger | **30–80 ms**, children in reading order |
| Trigger | IntersectionObserver, `-12%` bottom root margin, **fires once** |

- **A fade with no rise reads as a loading glitch.** A rise **past 24 px reads
  as a slide.** 14 px is the band, not a starting point to tune upward.
- The `-12%` margin fires the reveal when the reader is looking, not when the
  first pixel clears the fold.
- `data-sc-in` is what the engine watches. Without it nothing fires and the
  stagger children stay hidden.
- **Content that re-hides on the way back up is a defect, not an effect.**
- *"Larger, slower, or bouncier is never more premium; the restraint is the
  signal."*

**A flow section directly after a pinned act takes reduced padding.** The
pinned stage needs a full viewport to scroll off, and full `--sc-section`
padding on top of that delays the flow section's first content by another
screen. The harness will not call it dead scroll — correctly, the stage is
moving — and the reader still sees a near-empty screen. Cut the block padding
there and start the first reveal near `p = 0`.

## Rail settle on `pan` (§3)

Lateral travel alone reads as a slideshow on rails. **Give the rail's items a
staggered settle driven from `--sc-p`** and they read as a drawer being
pulled instead.

- **Exempt the first item** — a `pan` act needs its opening content already
  present.
- **Floor the opacity around 0.55**, so a not-yet-settled card reads as
  arriving rather than as failing to load.

Upstream gates the settle to `prefers-reduced-motion` — **utgår, F-011**.
The settle always runs. What *does* survive from
the same passage is the reachability requirement, which is not a motion
preference at all: a `pan` rail's transform **is** the navigation, so nothing
may zero it and park the act on its first screenful. Every item in a rail
stays reachable, and that is checked on the sheet, not assumed.

Two more, from the same section:

- **Card copy is read while cropped.** Items enter and leave through the
  viewport edges, so a heading is half-shown for most of its life, and two
  half-headings side by side can read as a third word (`TRACE` beside
  `EVALUATE` becoming `RE EVALUATE`). Keep card headings to one or two short
  words and expect every line to be read partially cut off.
- If three items do not reach half a viewport of overflow, **the fix is more
  rail, not wider cards**: put the act's heading in as the first item and a
  closing note as the last. Both earn their place, and they add the width the
  travel needs.

## Devices that cannot share an element (§9)

**`magnet`, `parallax` and `cue` all write `transform`.** The magnet writes
every frame in its own rAF loop, so it silently wins and the cue's entrance
rise is discarded — a visible animation lost to a race, with nothing in the
console.

- On a magnetic CTA, set **`data-sc-rise="0"`** so the cue writes a no-op
  instead of losing to the magnet.
- A cued element that wants its own continuous transform drives an **inner
  wrapper** from `--sc-p` in CSS, rather than stacking a second device on the
  same node.

All three pointer devices **interpolate toward** the pointer rather than
tracking it directly: *"direct tracking reads as artificial because it carries
no momentum."* They stay gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` so
touch never fires a false hover — that gate is a pointer-capability query, not
a motion preference, and it stands.
The reduced-motion half of the same sentence does not port (F-011).

## Kinetic type: the mask and the re-split (§5)

Each unit slides up from **behind a mask**, so it enters from a clean edge
rather than simply fading.

- **Line masks must reserve room for descenders.** A mask clipped to the line
  box shears the tails off g, y, p and j, *"and that is the single most common
  way this effect looks broken."*
- **Line splitting measures real line boxes, so it re-runs after
  `document.fonts.ready`.** Do not call it on text still loading its face. The
  same `fonts.ready` handle earns its place twice over: a webfont swapping in
  changes the measured height of every copy block, so anything sized against
  those blocks (a scrim plate, a rail) is wrong until it re-measures.
- Lines are almost always right; words for a short punch line; characters
  approximately never, *"because it turns reading into waiting."*
- **One kinetic headline per act, at most.**

## What makes a `count` land (§7)

- **Ease out, hard.** A cubic ease-out, so most of the distance goes by in the
  first third and the last digits settle slowly. *"A linear count reads as a
  slot machine."*
- **1.2–1.8 s.** Under a second and the reader misses that it moved; past two
  and they are waiting for a number they have already guessed.
- **Fires at half visibility, once**, so the reader is looking at it when it
  starts, and it never re-runs on the way back up.
- **Pair it with the fade.** A counter inside a `data-sc-in` stack rises in
  with its label and starts ticking as it arrives — *"the same numbers static
  on the page read as a spreadsheet."*
- Write the target exactly as it should render, commas included; the engine
  strips them before parsing and applies `tabular-nums` so the layout does not
  jitter.

**A concept, fictional or pre-launch brand has no verified figures, so it has
no counters.** The device suits a SaaS or agency page and will look good in
the score table, *"which is exactly the trap: every number you could put in it
would be invented."* Decide this before designing an act around a number, not
after. Real brand, real stats, or a different device.

## Appendix: pattern vocabulary

Named patterns from taste-skill § 10, carried here so orchestrator, builder
and reviewer name the same thing. It is a **vocabulary, not a menu** — several
entries below are banned as directions elsewhere in the chain (glassmorphism,
holographic foil, carousels, gooey menus) and appear here only so a critique
can say which trope it is refusing.

- **Hero** — Asymmetric Split · Editorial Manifesto · Video/Media Mask ·
  Kinetic-Type · Curtain-Reveal · Scroll-Pinned.
- **Nav** — Dock Magnification · Magnetic Button (`data-sc-magnet`) · Gooey
  Menu · Dynamic Island · Contextual Radial · Floating Speed Dial · Mega Menu
  Reveal.
- **Layout** — Bento Grid · Masonry · Chroma Grid · Split-Screen Scroll ·
  Sticky-Stack Sections.
- **Cards** — Parallax Tilt Card (`data-sc-tilt`) · Spotlight Border Card
  (`data-sc-spotlight`) · Glassmorphism Panel · Holographic Foil ·
  Tinder Swipe Stack · Morphing Modal.
- **Scroll** — Sticky Scroll Stack · Horizontal Scroll Hijack (= `pan`) ·
  Locomotive / Sequence Scroll (= `scrub`) · Zoom Parallax · Scroll Progress
  Path · Liquid Swipe Transition.
- **Galleries** — Dome Gallery · Coverflow Carousel · Drag-to-Pan Grid ·
  Accordion Image Slider · Hover Image Trail · Glitch Effect Image.
- **Type** — Kinetic Marquee · **Text Mask Reveal** (massive type as a
  transparent window onto video — this is K2's letter-window) · Text Scramble
  · Circular Text Path · Gradient Stroke Animation · Kinetic Typography Grid.
- **Micro** — Particle Explosion Button · Liquid Pull-to-Refresh · Skeleton
  Shimmer · Directional Hover-Aware Button · Ripple Click · Animated SVG Line
  Drawing · Mesh Gradient Background · Lens Blur Depth.

Names alone are not permission. A pattern still has to clear the fingerprint
gate, the register, and `../motion.md` before it ships.

## Never restyle the engine's classes (AB06, 2026-09-03)

Theme the engine only through its six colour tokens and two fonts. A project rule on
`.sc-stage`, `.sc-copy`, `.sc-scrim` or any other `.sc-*` class silently wins over the
engine: the console then says `[scrollcraft] act "…" will not pin: its stage computes
position:relative` and every pinned act scrolls away, leaving its spacer as dead scroll.
Read the console for `[scrollcraft]` warnings before anything else in Step 5, and run
`scripts/scroll_verify.py` — a blind one-shot cannot see either. The engine is opt-in per
grammar (scrub, pin, pan); a page that keeps the chain's own single set-piece + shared
reveal does not need it.

46	
47	Complete, before building: *"it's the site where ___."* "It has a scrub
48	video" is a device name — no hook. "You drag the letters of the logo apart
49	and they snap back perfectly" is an experience — that's a hook. The blank has

51	contains the signature move; if the tell-someone sentence and the signature
52	move point at different moments, one of them is decoration.

55	
56	One bespoke interaction that exists on this build alone — coded in the page
57	off `--sc-p` or a page-authored `data-sc-*`, never a parameter on a kit
58	device, never in any prior build. The engine stays untouched.
59	
60	**What counts** (upstream examples, not a menu to pick from): scroll-as-
61	playhead over a persistent trace rail; a wordmark the pointer pulls apart and
62	snaps back exactly; a line drawing whose `stroke-dashoffset` is driven from
63	`--sc-p`; a running receipt that accumulates real figures; one control that
64	regrades the whole page at once (time-of-day, temperature, load).
65

67	up; a different easing on kinetic lines; more cards in a rail; a third
68	`scrub` act; anything the engine already does under a project class name.

70	can't tell it apart from something the kit already does, it isn't one.
71	
72	## Being in it, not watching it
73	
74	Upstream `feel.md` § 4. *"A film plays whether you are there or not. The
75	difference between a viewer and a participant is whether the page acknowledges
76	that somebody specific is here: how fast they are moving, where their pointer
77	is, whether they stopped."*
78	
79	Five techniques, in the kit's own vocabulary:
80	
81	- **Pointer parallax that moves the world, not a card.** `data-sc-spotlight`
82	  publishes `--sc-mx` / `--sc-my`. Drive a *background layer's* transform off
83	  them instead of a highlight, and the environment shifts as the visitor
84	  moves, slightly, the way a real space does when you lean.
85	- **Dwell-triggered detail.** Hold still on an act and something further
86	  arrives — a caption, a second line, a small annotation. Reward for stopping.
87	  Mechanically: **read `--sc-p` staying constant across a few frames**, in the
88	  page's own JS, and reveal something that was **never needed for
89	  comprehension**.
90	- **Scroll velocity shaping intensity.** Fast scrolling raises grain, blur,
91	  chromatic offset, ground saturation; slow scrolling settles it. *"The page
92	  feels like it is being driven rather than played back, and it costs one
93	  derived custom property."*
94	- **The page addressing "you" at one moment that lands.** Not throughout,
95	  which is just copywriting. **One line**, at the emotional turn, in second
96	  person, when the visitor is already implicated. *"It works because it is the
97	  only time."*
98	- **A trace of where they have been.** Anything that accumulates as they
99	  travel, so arriving at the end means having a record rather than reaching a
100	  footer.
101	
102	**Embodiment is seasoning. One or two per page.** *"A page that reacts to
103	everything feels haunted, not alive: the visitor stops reading and starts
104	poking, which is the opposite of what any of this is for."* Pick the one that
105	serves the peak and leave the rest.
106	
107	These are gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` — a pointer-capability
108	query, which stands.
109	Upstream also turns them off under reduced motion — **that half utgår, F-011**.
110	The rule that does survive is upstream's own:
111	*"a technique that only exists on desktop cannot be the thing that carries the
112	page's meaning."*
113	
114	## Pacing as emotion
115	
116	Upstream `feel.md` § 5. *"Scroll distance is emotional time. It is the only
117	clock this medium has, and it is fully under your control, which makes it the
118	cheapest emotional instrument in the kit and the one most often left at
119	default."*
120	
121	| Pacing | Reads as | Built with |
122	|---|---|---|
123	| Short acts, hard cuts | Adrenaline, pulse, impatience | Acts under 1.4 vh, no `pin`, `dwell` at 0 |
124	| A long pin | Held breath, pressure, attention | `data-sc-span` 3+, overlapping cues, one idea |
125	| An empty viewport before a reveal | Silence before the drop | A ground-only act, no cue until the next one |
126	| A slow settle mid-act | The shot landing | `data-sc-dwell` 0.35–0.6, cue peak on the settle |
127	| A fast cue with a long plateau | Confidence, arrival | `data-sc-cue="0.1 0.9 0.08 0.4"` |
128	| A slow ramp in | Hesitation, dawning | Long `rampIn` — **once per page**, it is close to feeling broken |
129

131	
132	- **Silence must be authored, not left over.** *"An empty screen you meant
133	  reads as anticipation. An empty screen you did not mean reads as a page that
134	  failed to load, and the harness reports both as dead scroll."* If the empty
135	  viewport before the peak is deliberate, **say so in `BRIEF.md`** so the
136	  verification pass can tell it from dead scroll. This is the sentence that
137	  keeps `scroll_verify.py`'s `blankBands` check from being either useless or a
138	  false alarm.
139	- **Give the peak room.** The peak act has the largest span on the page by a
140	  visible margin. *"If every act is 2.2 vh, the page has no shape, whatever
141	  the curve in BRIEF.md says."*
142	- **Compress the administrative parts.** Specs, logistics, FAQ, credentials
143	  are information, not experience — flow sections at short stagger, never
144	  pinned acts with dwell. Spending scroll on them spends the visitor's
145	  patience on the part they will not remember.
146	- **A continuous world is the exception to pacing variety.** All of the above
147	  is about a page of *acts*. A worldflight is one camera move, and *"a camera
148	  that changes speed between legs reads as broken rather than as
149	  expressive."* There, hold one pace and let the peak carry the shape by being
150	  the single long leg — [`pace.md`](pace.md).
151	
152	The total-length budget stays **8–14 viewport-heights**. Pacing is how that
153	budget is spent, not permission to spend more: *"a page that needs 20 vh to
154	land its curve has too many acts, not too little room."*
155	
156	## The fingerprint gate
157	
158	Registry: `VAULT/wiki/projects/_index/design-fingerprints.md`, per-vault,
159	starting from whatever rows already exist — not repeating **yourself** across
160	builds, not a universal constraint. **Six dimensions**, recorded per row:
161	
162	| # | Dimension | What it records |
163	|---|---|---|
164	| 1 | Grammar | Which of `grammars.md`, or a named new one |
165	| 2 | Nav treatment | What the chrome is and what it's for |
166	| 3 | Hero device | What the first screen does |
167	| 4 | Act-sequence shape | Device order, act count, total viewport-heights |
168	| 5 | Close pattern | How the last screen behaves, what the CTA sits in |
169	| 6 | Signature move | The one bespoke interaction, in a phrase |
170	
171	**The gate: a new build must differ from EVERY existing row on at least 4 of
172	the 6** — four against each row individually, not averaged across the table.
173	Dimension 6 is free (unique by definition), so the gate really asks for 3
174	more out of the remaining 5 against each row. If the plan fails, **change
175	the plan, not the log** — rewriting a row to fit is what makes it worthless.
176	
177	**Row format** — one row per shipped build, all six dimensions plus a world
178	note and the path: `| Build | Grammar | Nav | Hero device | Act-sequence
179	shape | Close pattern | Signature move | Register | World / palette | Path |`
180	
181	**Rows are append-only.** From upstream `templates/FINGERPRINTS.md`:
182	
183	> *"A build that has been superseded stays in the table, because the space it
184	> occupies is still occupied."*
185	
186	A replaced, retired or rejected build keeps its row. The registry does not
187	record what is live; it records what surface has already been taken, and a
188	surface stays taken whether or not the build that claimed it is still up.
189	Deleting a row silently frees a shape for reuse, which is the same failure as
190	editing one to make room — *"never edit a row to make room for it. If a
191	planned build fails, change the plan."*
192	
193	**Fill every column.** A row with blanks cannot be scored 4-of-6 against, so
194	it weakens the gate for every build after it.
195	
196	**Keep a "what is taken" list beside the table.** Add a bullet whenever a
197	build claims something a later build should avoid reusing: a grammar, a nav
198	treatment, a close pattern, a signature move, an act-count-and-length band.
199	*"The shared columns are what the next build inherits as a constraint, so
200	writing them down is the whole point."*
201	
202	After shipping, append the row and say what it shares with prior rows — the
203	shared columns are exactly what the *next* build has to avoid.

  moves, slightly, the way a real space does when you lean.
- **Dwell-triggered detail.** Hold still on an act and something further
  arrives — a caption, a second line, a small annotation. Reward for stopping.
  Mechanically: **read `--sc-p` staying constant across a few frames**, in the
  page's own JS, and reveal something that was **never needed for
  comprehension**.
- **Scroll velocity shaping intensity.** Fast scrolling raises grain, blur,
  chromatic offset, ground saturation; slow scrolling settles it. *"The page
  feels like it is being driven rather than played back, and it costs one
  derived custom property."*
- **The page addressing "you" at one moment that lands.** Not throughout,
  which is just copywriting. **One line**, at the emotional turn, in second
  person, when the visitor is already implicated. *"It works because it is the
  only time."*
- **A trace of where they have been.** Anything that accumulates as they
  travel, so arriving at the end means having a record rather than reaching a
  footer.

**Embodiment is seasoning. One or two per page.** *"A page that reacts to
everything feels haunted, not alive: the visitor stops reading and starts
poking, which is the opposite of what any of this is for."* Pick the one that
serves the peak and leave the rest.

These are gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` — a pointer-capability
query, which stands.
Upstream also turns them off under reduced motion — **that half utgår, F-011**.
The rule that does survive is upstream's own:
*"a technique that only exists on desktop cannot be the thing that carries the
page's meaning."*

## Pacing as emotion

Upstream `feel.md` § 5. *"Scroll distance is emotional time. It is the only
clock this medium has, and it is fully under your control, which makes it the
cheapest emotional instrument in the kit and the one most often left at
default."*

| Pacing | Reads as | Built with |
|---|---|---|
| Short acts, hard cuts | Adrenaline, pulse, impatience | Acts under 1.4 vh, no `pin`, `dwell` at 0 |
| A long pin | Held breath, pressure, attention | `data-sc-span` 3+, overlapping cues, one idea |
| An empty viewport before a reveal | Silence before the drop | A ground-only act, no cue until the next one |
| A slow settle mid-act | The shot landing | `data-sc-dwell` 0.35–0.6, cue peak on the settle |
| A fast cue with a long plateau | Confidence, arrival | `data-sc-cue="0.1 0.9 0.08 0.4"` |
| A slow ramp in | Hesitation, dawning | Long `rampIn` — **once per page**, it is close to feeling broken |

Four rules follow:

- **Silence must be authored, not left over.** *"An empty screen you meant
  reads as anticipation. An empty screen you did not mean reads as a page that
  failed to load, and the harness reports both as dead scroll."* If the empty
  viewport before the peak is deliberate, **say so in `BRIEF.md`** so the
  verification pass can tell it from dead scroll. This is the sentence that
  keeps `scroll_verify.py`'s `blankBands` check from being either useless or a
  false alarm.
- **Give the peak room.** The peak act has the largest span on the page by a
  visible margin. *"If every act is 2.2 vh, the page has no shape, whatever
  the curve in BRIEF.md says."*
- **Compress the administrative parts.** Specs, logistics, FAQ, credentials
  are information, not experience — flow sections at short stagger, never
  pinned acts with dwell. Spending scroll on them spends the visitor's
  patience on the part they will not remember.
- **A continuous world is the exception to pacing variety.** All of the above
  is about a page of *acts*. A worldflight is one camera move, and *"a camera
  that changes speed between legs reads as broken rather than as
  expressive."* There, hold one pace and let the peak carry the shape by being
  the single long leg — [`pace.md`](pace.md).

The total-length budget stays **8–14 viewport-heights**. Pacing is how that
budget is spent, not permission to spend more: *"a page that needs 20 vh to
land its curve has too many acts, not too little room."*

## The fingerprint gate

Registry: `VAULT/wiki/projects/_index/design-fingerprints.md`, per-vault,
starting from whatever rows already exist — not repeating **yourself** across
builds, not a universal constraint. **Six dimensions**, recorded per row:

| # | Dimension | What it records |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Grammar | Which of `grammars.md`, or a named new one |
| 2 | Nav treatment | What the chrome is and what it's for |
| 3 | Hero device | What the first screen does |
| 4 | Act-sequence shape | Device order, act count, total viewport-heights |
| 5 | Close pattern | How the last screen behaves, what the CTA sits in |
| 6 | Signature move | The one bespoke interaction, in a phrase |

**The gate: a new build must differ from EVERY existing row on at least 4 of
the 6** — four against each row individually, not averaged across the table.
Dimension 6 is free (unique by definition), so the gate really asks for 3
more out of the remaining 5 against each row. If the plan fails, **change
the plan, not the log** — rewriting a row to fit is what makes it worthless.

**Row format** — one row per shipped build, all six dimensions plus a world
note and the path: `| Build | Grammar | Nav | Hero device | Act-sequence
shape | Close pattern | Signature move | Register | World / palette | Path |`

**Rows are append-only.** From upstream `templates/FINGERPRINTS.md`:

> *"A build that has been superseded stays in the table, because the space it
> occupies is still occupied."*

A replaced, retired or rejected build keeps its row. The registry does not
record what is live; it records what surface has already been taken, and a
surface stays taken whether or not the build that claimed it is still up.
Deleting a row silently frees a shape for reuse, which is the same failure as
editing one to make room — *"never edit a row to make room for it. If a
planned build fails, change the plan."*

**Fill every column.** A row with blanks cannot be scored 4-of-6 against, so
it weakens the gate for every build after it.

**Keep a "what is taken" list beside the table.** Add a bullet whenever a
build claims something a later build should avoid reusing: a grammar, a nav
treatment, a close pattern, a signature move, an act-count-and-length band.
*"The shared columns are what the next build inherits as a constraint, so
writing them down is the whole point."*

After shipping, append the row and say what it shares with prior rows — the
shared columns are exactly what the *next* build has to avoid.

43	  the second profile and belongs to ordinary flow sections on a scroll page:
44	  **opacity from 0, a rise of about 14px over 620ms on an ease-out curve, 30–80ms
45	  stagger through the children in reading order, triggered slightly inside the
46	  viewport (`-12%` bottom root margin)** so it fires when the reader is looking
47	  rather than when the first pixel clears the fold. Its two failure bounds are
48	  exact and worth memorising: **a fade with no rise reads as a loading glitch; a
49	  rise past 24px reads as a slide.** *"Larger, slower, or bouncier is never more
50	  premium; the restraint is the signal."* **Conflict, resolved:** these are not
51	  competing values for the same thing — 28px/1.3s is the shared *page* reveal in
52	  the editorial registers, 14px/620ms is the *section* reveal on a scroll build,

65	  tabular mono is what makes a column of them scannable (stitch

67	  mono numeral in a 3-density editorial page is apparatus, and the apparatus

92	  `layout-and-space.md` § Optical adjustments derives values *from* this
93	  vocabulary rather than adding to it.
94	- **The worked example of a coordinated two-layer set-piece** is

97	  is held on `delay-300` so it starts *after* the arrow arrives. That delayed

99	  on the first, so the motion reads as one gesture with a cause instead of two

25	
26	## Why it works
27	
28	The hero borrows interface language from software, not marketing: a
29	`(EST. 2019 — VERSION 1.0.4)` tag, a corner-marked grid frame around the
30	wordmark card, a live local-time readout, and an availability counter
31	("Slots for APR: |||||  2 left"). None of this is a real product — it's an
32	agency's own homepage — but framing the studio itself as a versioned, in-stock
33	piece of software borrows urgency and precision language from a different
34	category entirely.
35	
36	A founder photo and signature sit inside the same framed card as the wordmark,
37	which personalises what would otherwise be a purely systemic, cold hero. It's a
38	small human anchor inside a page that otherwise leans hard on grid lines,
39	timestamps and version numbers.
40	
41	The page then commits fully to one flat, saturated orange for an entire
42	full-bleed section — a bold three-word thesis ("STRATEGY BEFORE PIXELS.") set
43	in huge condensed type beside a black-and-white fashion-editorial photograph
44	and a single stat ("12+ Industries"). The colour block does more branding work
45	in one screen than a logo could, simply by being the loudest, most confident
46	thing on the page.
47	
48	## What to borrow (principle)
49	
50	- **Frame your own homepage like a software product**, with a version tag, a
51	  live clock, and an availability counter, to borrow precision and urgency
52	  language from a different category.
53	- **Put a founder photo and signature inside the hero's framed card**, not in a
54	  separate "about" section, to personalise an otherwise systemic layout.

---
title: "Mattis Studio (agency template)"
url: https://mattis.framer.website/
source_url: https://mattis.framer.website/
captured: 2026-09-04
origin: raw-url
extract: ok
raw: raw/bd32f41ebcc487db-screenshot-upload.webp
category: portfolio
category2: ""
family: grid-boxed-console-agency
dna: "Software changelog framing x design/dev agency pitch"
register: cinematic dark
grammar: split stage
lane: "A black hero framed like a software console — version tag, live clock, slot counter — opens the page, then a single orange full-bleed block states the studio's thesis beside a fashion photograph, closing on plain grey display type"
mode: persuade
traits: ["grid-boxed console-style hero framing", "version-number tag", "live local-time clock", "availability slot counter", "founder signature overlay", "bold orange full-bleed thesis block", "fashion-editorial photography", "oversized flat-colour headline blocks", "condensed bold sans display"]
palette: ["#0B0B0B", "#F04E23", "#FFFFFF", "#E7E5E1", "#1C1C1C"]
type: ["Geist"]
measured: designlang (confirmed)
kind: reference-style
source: anton
status: ready
---

## Why it works

The hero borrows interface language from software, not marketing: a
`(EST. 2019 — VERSION 1.0.4)` tag, a corner-marked grid frame around the
wordmark card, a live local-time readout, and an availability counter
("Slots for APR: |||||  2 left"). None of this is a real product — it's an
agency's own homepage — but framing the studio itself as a versioned, in-stock
piece of software borrows urgency and precision language from a different
category entirely.

A founder photo and signature sit inside the same framed card as the wordmark,
which personalises what would otherwise be a purely systemic, cold hero. It's a
small human anchor inside a page that otherwise leans hard on grid lines,
timestamps and version numbers.

The page then commits fully to one flat, saturated orange for an entire
full-bleed section — a bold three-word thesis ("STRATEGY BEFORE PIXELS.") set
in huge condensed type beside a black-and-white fashion-editorial photograph
and a single stat ("12+ Industries"). The colour block does more branding work
in one screen than a logo could, simply by being the loudest, most confident
thing on the page.

## What to borrow (principle)

- **Frame your own homepage like a software product**, with a version tag, a
  live clock, and an availability counter, to borrow precision and urgency
  language from a different category.
- **Put a founder photo and signature inside the hero's framed card**, not in a
  separate "about" section, to personalise an otherwise systemic layout.
- **Commit an entire section to one flat saturated colour** for your core thesis
  statement — it reads as more confident than a colour used sparingly.
- **Pair a black-and-white editorial photograph against a saturated colour
  block** rather than a colour photograph, so the photo and the colour don't
  compete.

## What to leave

- A "slots left this month" counter is a scarcity device borrowed from
  consumer/booking products; for a design agency it can read as a gimmick
  unless the scarcity is genuinely real and updated.
- The console-style hero (version tag, clock, grid frame) is dense with small
  metadata that risks distracting from the actual value proposition on first
  glance — it rewards a second look more than a first one.

## Signature move

The versioned, grid-framed hero card: the studio's name and pitch live inside a
bordered card with corner marks (like a UI component being inspected),
carrying a version number, a founder signature, and a live clock — treating the
agency's own brand as a piece of software with a release history.

## Motion

(from designlang extract) Feel is "mixed" with scroll-linked motion confirmed,
though the captured CSS is thin: a `200ms` custom ease
(`cubic-bezier(0.44,0,0.56,1)`, a near-symmetric ease-in-out, 15 uses) drives
link/underline colour changes, plus the framework's `1ms` allow-discrete
overflow transition. The one keyframe present is a generic loading spinner —
no clock-tick or card-select animation was captured, so that read from the
image stays inferred rather than confirmed.

| token | value | role |
|---|---|---|
| `instant` | 1ms | framework overflow transition |
| `sm` | 200ms | link/underline colour changes |
| custom | `cubic-bezier(0.44,0,0.56,1)` | only family found (15 uses) |

## Brief

Build a dark, systems-minded agency homepage. Frame the hero as a bordered card
with corner marks, a version tag, a live local-time clock, and an availability
counter, with the founder's photo and signature inside the same card. Set the
studio name in a large bold wordmark within that frame. Immediately after,
commit one full-bleed section to a single flat saturated colour carrying a
three-to-five-word thesis statement in huge condensed type, paired with one
black-and-white editorial photograph and a single stat. Close on plain,
oversized display type stating what the studio actually builds.

## Image recipe

Black-and-white editorial fashion photograph of [SUBJECT], studio-lit, high
contrast, one figure in three-quarter or profile pose against a plain
background, shot to read as confident and slightly detached rather than warm
or candid.

## Photo search

Unsplash first, Pexels second.
- "black and white fashion editorial studio"
- "monochrome portrait high contrast studio"
- "editorial fashion photography plain background"

## Reference lock

Primary reference/direction: Mattis Studio — versioned software-style hero card with a founder signature, breaking into one flat-colour thesis block with black-and-white editorial photography.
Preserve (3-5 traits): hero framed as a bordered, corner-marked card carrying a version tag and live clock; founder photo and signature placed inside that same card, not a separate section; one full-bleed section committed entirely to a single flat saturated colour for the core thesis; black-and-white (not colour) photography paired against the saturated colour block.
Borrow only (1-2): the "slots left this month" availability counter, used only if genuinely accurate; the single stat paired with the thesis block.
Role rules: only one saturated flat-colour section per page; photography stays black-and-white wherever it meets a saturated colour block; version/clock metadata stays confined to the hero card, never repeated elsewhere.
Media strategy: photo:unsplash — black-and-white editorial/fashion photography only where paired with the saturated colour block; no colour photography elsewhere on the page.
Reject: a fabricated scarcity counter that doesn't reflect real availability; colour photography competing against the flat saturated section; a hero card with no personal/human element.
Token commitments: black `#0B0B0B`, orange `#F04E23`, white `#FFFFFF`, grey `#E7E5E1`, dark-grey `#1C1C1C`; condensed bold sans for all display type.
